Creating Packages

This content was generated with the assistance of AI and should be verified against the official documentation before being relied on in production.

The reference material consulted while preparing these pages is listed in the section bibliography.

Checked against R 4.6.1 (2026-06-24) on 2026-10-20; R 4.6.2 is scheduled for 2026-10-29. The base R packages tools and utils do most of the work behind the commands on this page. The add-on packages that drive them were checked at these versions: usethis 3.2.2, devtools 2.5.2, roxygen2 8.1.1, testthat 3.3.2, knitr 1.52, rmarkdown 2.32, withr 3.0.3, lintr 3.4.0, pkgload 1.5.3 and fs 2.1.0. devtools builds and checks through pkgbuild 1.4.8, rcmdcheck 1.4.0 and pak 0.11.1, and covr 3.6.5 measured the test coverage that is mentioned once. Four more packages appear only as names in a deliberately broken copy of the package or in one dependency demonstration: jsonlite 2.0.0, stringr 1.6.0, Rcpp 1.1.2 and MASS 7.3-65. Everything else is base R.

A package is the unit in which R code is shared: a directory with a DESCRIPTION file that says what the code is, a NAMESPACE file that says which names it offers and which it borrows, and the code, documentation, data and tests that belong with it. This page explains what each part of that directory is for, which fields and directives R understands, how the usual tools write them, and how a source directory becomes something other people can install. The same steps are then done by hand with the R CMD commands that ship with R, so that nothing about the tooling is a mystery when it prints a warning.

Every example is a script that was run with Rscript on R 4.6.1 with warnings printed as they happen (options(warn = 1)), and the lines that start with #> are what it printed. The scripts pass the default lintr linters. The package that the page builds is called shelf. It is the analysis side of the running library-shelf scenario described on the section index: the same books and loans data frames, the same book class and the same overdue-loan analyses, packaged. It was created, documented, tested, built and checked for real with the tools on this page, and its files are shown as the tools wrote them (the R code of the step-by-step section as excerpts). The package directory is written ~/shelf throughout, and the longer absolute paths that some messages print were shortened to it ("paths shortened"). Blocks that show a file of the package (R/book.R, DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE) are package sources, not scripts: they define functions and metadata for the package and are not run by Rscript; they were checked with lintr’s lint_package(), which sees the whole package at once. Blocks that show the calls of the recorded creation session (the usethis steps) are fragments of that one session, and the text before them says so. Check output is shown without its first lines: the platform header (the operating system, the compiler, the time and the temporary directory) is left out, and every check step that is shown comes from the real run.

The page is the first of the package pages. Packages, Libraries and Namespaces explains how to use other people’s packages (libraries, attaching, ::). Documentation with Rd, roxygen2 and Vignettes writes the help pages and vignettes of shelf, Testing with testthat writes its tests, and Publishing to CRAN takes the finished package to CRAN. Here the subject is the package itself: its structure, its metadata and the road from source to installed.

What a package is

R’s own manual defines the word precisely, and the rest of the page depends on the definition. A package is a directory of files that extend R, and the manual distinguishes three things that people all call "the package": the source package (the master files), a tarball that contains the files of a source package, and the installed package, which is the result of running R CMD INSTALL on a source package. On some platforms there is a fourth, a binary package: a compressed copy of an installed package that can be unpacked instead of built. The R FAQ (question 5.5, "How can I create an R package?") gives the same list of subdirectories and files and says that a package consists of a subdirectory containing a file DESCRIPTION and the subdirectories R, data, demo, exec, inst, man, po, src and tests, some of which can be missing. R itself is distributed with about thirty packages (base, stats, utils, methods and the recommended ones), and they are built exactly like yours.

Two terms are easy to confuse. A package is not a library: a library is a directory into which packages are installed, so a library is a folder of package folders (R FAQ 7.29, "What is the difference between package and library?", says the same in one sentence: a package is a standardized collection of material extending R, and a library is a place where R knows to find packages). library(shelf) therefore means "find the package shelf in a library and load it". The other confusing word is "compile". Installing a package that contains C, C++ or Fortran code compiles that code, but a package of R code only is not compiled: R byte-compiles its functions on installation, which has been the default for every package since R 3.5.0 (the NEWS of R 3.5.0 lists it among the significant user-visible changes), and Writing R Extensions points out that compilation is not a correct term for a package of R code.

Why write a package at all, even for private code? A package gives a bundle of functions a name, a version and a place to live. Its namespace keeps its internal helpers from clashing with names in the user’s workspace and says what is public. Its documentation is checked against its code, so a renamed argument that nobody documented is reported. Its tests run in a clean session against the installed code. Its dependencies are declared, so installing it installs what it needs, and a missing dependency is an error at install time instead of a surprise at run time. The cost of all that was once a day of reading manuals, and it is now a few commands, which is why the usual advice is to turn a collection of scripts into a package as soon as a second project reuses it. A package does not have to be published: the same directory can be installed from a local path or from a tarball on a shared disk, and the rest of the page never needs a network.

The five states of a package

A package is not one thing but a thing in five different states. The community book R Packages (a free online book by the authors of the tools used below) names them: a source package, a bundled package, a binary package, an installed package and an in-memory package, and the page uses its vocabulary because it matches the manual. Each state is produced from an earlier one by one command, and every problem a package author meets happens at one of those steps, which is why the figure puts the command on each arrow. The left half of the figure is the directory that the next section opens, and the dashed boxes in it are the entries that R CMD build leaves out of the bundle.

State What it is Made by Used by

1. Source

A directory with the files edited by hand and by tools, ~/shelf here.

You, with usethis::create_package() and an editor.

devtools::load_all(), R CMD build shelf, R CMD INSTALL shelf.

2. Bundle

A single compressed file, shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz, called a tarball in the manuals. It is the source minus what .Rbuildignore excludes, plus the vignettes already built (inst/doc).

R CMD build shelf

R CMD check, CRAN, install.packages(type = "source"), R CMD INSTALL shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz.

3. Binary

A compressed copy of the installed package, specific to one operating system and R series; it holds the lazy-load databases, not the R source.

R CMD INSTALL --build shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz

install.packages() on a platform where binaries are the norm: users get no compiler requirement.

4. Installed

A folder inside a library (the first entry of .libPaths(), or the --library directory): R/, help/, Meta/, NAMESPACE, DESCRIPTION and the rest.

R CMD INSTALL, install.packages(), devtools::install()

library(), loadNamespace(), requireNamespace(), shelf::normalise_isbn().

5. In memory

The namespace loaded in a running session, with the package attached to the search path when library() did it.

library(shelf), loadNamespace("shelf"), or devtools::load_all() straight from state 1.

Your code.

Source: Writing R Extensions: Creating R packages

The steps are one-way and each one adds something. The build step runs the vignettes, because a bundle should not need knitr or pandoc on the machine that installs it. The install step lays the package out as R reads it: the code of R/ is evaluated once and stored in a lazy-load database (R/shelf.rdb and R/shelf.rdx), so loading the package does not run your top-level code again, and the help pages are converted into a database as well. A binary package is that installed layout in a tarball; the section on R CMD INSTALL lists its contents. The in-memory state is where almost all of the confusion about packages comes from: library() performs two steps, loading the namespace and attaching the package to the search path, and a namespace can be loaded without being attached, which is what shelf::normalise_isbn() does. The page returns to the difference when the load hooks are explained, and Packages, Libraries and Namespaces covers it from the user’s side.

Because the five states are different files, the same package can behave differently in two of them, and most "it works on my machine" reports are of this kind. A function that reads a file with a path relative to the source tree works under load_all() and fails when installed; a helper that is not exported is visible from inside the package and from a load_all() session but not to library() users; a dataset that was never saved into data/ exists in the author’s workspace and nowhere else. The tools below exist to test the package in the state the user will have it in, and the habit that pays is to run R CMD check on a bundle, because the bundle is the state in between that the rest of the world sees.

The anatomy of a package directory

The finished shelf source package is the directory below, listed with fs::dir_tree() from the package root, hidden files included. Every file in it was written by a tool or copied in as the step-by-step section shows; the only files written by hand are the contents of R/, data-raw/, tests/, vignettes/ and the text of NEWS.md and inst/CITATION.

# The source tree of the finished package, hidden files included.
fs::dir_tree(".", all = TRUE)

#> ├── .gitignore
#> ├── .lintr

Source: fs package documentation: dir_tree

Two files are the heart of every package and are not optional: DESCRIPTION and, in practice, NAMESPACE (every package has a namespace since R 2.14.0 in October 2011; if the author wrote no file, R CMD build creates a default one, as the NAMESPACE section shows). Everything else is a directory that R knows by name. Writing R Extensions lists the subdirectories that R reads: R, data, demo, exec, inst, man, po, src, tests, tools and vignettes; some of them can be missing, but none of them should be empty. The table gives each entry, what reads it, and what shelf puts there.

Entry What it is for In shelf

DESCRIPTION

The metadata: name, version, title, authors, licence, dependencies and the settings of tools. Read by library(), R CMD INSTALL, install.packages() and CRAN.

Shown in full below.

NAMESPACE

The exported and imported names and the S3 methods to register.

Written by roxygen2 from the @export tags.

R/

R code files only; the extension should be .R. Evaluated once, at installation. May hold sysdata.rda, the internal data.

book.R, clean.R, data.R, isbn.R, loans.R, zzz.R, sysdata.rda.

man/

Help pages in Rd format, one file per topic.

Nine .Rd files, written by roxygen2 from the comments above the functions.

tests/

Test code run by R CMD check.

testthat.R and testthat/, written by usethis::use_testthat().

data/

Datasets that users get with data() or, with LazyData, as soon as the package is attached.

books.rda, loans.rda.

data-raw/

Not an R convention: a place for the scripts and raw files that build data/. It is listed in .Rbuildignore, so it never reaches the bundle.

books.R and the two CSV files.

inst/

Files copied unchanged to the top of the installed package: CITATION, extdata/, built vignettes in inst/doc.

CITATION (the built vignette lands in inst/doc of the bundle).

vignettes/

Sources of the long-form guides.

shelf.Rmd.

src/

C, C++ or Fortran sources, with Makevars or Makefile.

None: shelf is R code only.

exec/, demo/, po/, tools/

Installed scripts, demos run by demo(), translation files and configure-time helpers.

None.

INDEX, configure, cleanup, LICENSE, NEWS

Optional files that R knows: a hand-written object index (normally generated), the Unix configure and cleanup scripts, the licence text and the news.

LICENSE, and NEWS.md.

.Rbuildignore

Regular expressions, one per line, for files that R CMD build must leave out.

Four patterns, discussed below.

Source: Writing R Extensions: Package structure

Writing R Extensions asks that the package subdirectory be given the same name as the package, that file names be portable (ASCII letters, digits, ., _ and a handful of other characters, no two names that differ only by case, no Windows device names such as con or aux), and that a package not contain Unix-style hidden files, with a few exceptions that the tools need. The tree above has several (.Rbuildignore, .gitignore, .lintr and vignettes/.gitignore), and the build handles them in different ways: .Rbuildignore is read by R CMD build and left out of the bundle, together with the files of version-control tools such as .gitignore, and .lintr is excluded by a pattern of .Rbuildignore itself. .Rinstignore is the exception that goes the other way: it is shipped, because it is read at installation. Any other hidden file is bundled, and the check reports it, as the real run below shows.

The R/ directory

The R code files are read in the C locale’s alphabetical order, so the order in which functions are defined does not matter for a function that is only called later: a function body is evaluated when it is called, not when it is defined. The manual says that it should be possible to read the files with source(), that the files should assign R objects and not call functions with side effects such as library(), require() or options(), and that there need be no connection between a file name and the objects defined in it. shelf follows the common practice of one file per topic (book.R for the class, isbn.R for ISBN handling, clean.R, loans.R) and a file called zzz.R for the load hooks, which sorts last.

There is a consequence of this rule that surprises everyone once. The files are evaluated at installation, and the objects they create are stored in the installed package, so a top-level expression is computed once, when the package is installed, not every time it is loaded. A definition of today’s date at the top level of a file freezes the date of the installation into the package. That is why shelf defines shelf_today(), a function that returns the current date and is evaluated when it is called (the same function can be replaced in tests, a trick the testing page uses), and why overdue_loans() takes today as an argument.

Where the order of the files does matter, for example when a top-level call in one file needs an object that another file creates, or when an S4 class must exist before its methods, the Collate field of DESCRIPTION lists the order. Writing it by hand is error-prone, so roxygen2 writes it from @include tags; the DESCRIPTION section shows the real result.

Only ASCII characters should appear in the code files. Other characters are accepted in comments, but the comments may not read correctly in every locale, and non-ASCII characters in object names normally fail at installation. A string that needs a non-ASCII character is written with a \u escape, and R CMD check warns about the rest ("checking code files for non-ASCII characters" in the section on reading the output of R CMD check, which shows the real warning).

The man/ directory

The man/ subdirectory holds the help pages, in R’s own documentation format Rd, one .Rd file per topic. R CMD check compares them with the code: every exported object must have an entry, every argument in \usage must be described, and the \usage must match the function’s real signature (the steps named "checking for missing documentation entries" and "checking for code/documentation mismatches" in the log). Nobody writes Rd files by hand any more. roxygen2 turns the comments above each function into them, which is why the first line of every file in man/ says "% Generated by roxygen2: do not edit by hand". Rd itself, the tags and the vignettes are the subject of Documentation with Rd, roxygen2 and Vignettes, and this page only uses them.

The tests/ directory

R CMD check runs the R files in tests/ in a clean session with the package installed, and compares each output with a .Rout.save file if there is one. testthat’s convention is one tiny file, tests/testthat.R, that loads the package and calls test_check("shelf"), and a directory tests/testthat/ of test-*.R files, helper files and fixtures. The same call is made by devtools::test(), which runs the tests against the loaded source. The details are the subject of Testing with testthat; for this page it is enough to know that the tests are part of the package and are executed by the check, and that R CMD check --no-tests skips them.

The vignettes/ directory

A vignette is a long-form document that is part of the package: a tutorial that runs real code against the package. The sources live in vignettes/, R CMD build runs them and stores the output in inst/doc of the bundle, and R CMD INSTALL installs that output. The VignetteBuilder field names the package that knows how to run them (knitr here), and that package, and rmarkdown for the html_vignette output, must be in Suggests. The build runs the vignettes with the package installed into a temporary library, which is why the build log says "installing the package (it is needed to build vignettes)". A tree that has vignettes/ but a bundle without inst/doc is reported by the check, as the section on reading the output of R CMD check shows.

The src/ directory and compiled code

A package can contain C, C++ and Fortran sources in src/. When it is installed, make compiles them into one shared object that R loads with the namespace, using useDynLib() in NAMESPACE. Compiled code needs the dependency field LinkingTo for header-only packages such as Rcpp, a NeedsCompilation field set by the build, and a compiler on the machine that installs the package from source (Rtools on Windows, the Xcode command-line tools on macOS). shelf has no src/ and the page treats the subject in one place: the DESCRIPTION and NAMESPACE sections name the fields and directives, and Interfacing C, C++ and Fortran writes the code.

exec/, demo/, po/ and tools/

Four more directories are rarely needed and are named here so that their names are not a surprise. exec/ holds scripts that the package needs at run time for an interpreter other than R (a shell, Perl or Python script): only files are installed from it, and they are marked executable. The manual remarks that most packages put such files in inst/ instead, because exec/ is not suited to compiled programs (installed packages can serve several architectures). demo/ holds R scripts that demo() runs, with a 00Index file listing them; they are not run by R CMD check unless it is asked to (--run-demo, added in R 4.5.0). po/ holds the translation files for the messages of a package, which Writing R Extensions covers in the chapter on internationalization. tools/ is the preferred place for auxiliary files needed while configuring a package that has a configure script.

The .Rbuildignore file

.Rbuildignore lists, one regular expression per line, the files and directories that R CMD build must not put in the bundle. The expressions are Perl-like and are matched case-insensitively against each path relative to the package root. Because they are regular expressions and not file globs, a dot must be escaped and the two ends should be anchored with ^ and $. shelf has these four lines, written by the usethis functions that created the files they refer to (use_mit_license(), use_data_raw(), use_cran_comments() and lintr::use_lintr()).

^LICENSE\.md$
^data-raw$
^cran-comments\.md$
^\.lintr$

Source: Writing R Extensions: Building package tarballs

The script below applies those patterns to a list of paths the way the build does, to make the anchoring visible. LICENSE.md and license.MD are excluded (the matching ignores case), the directory data-raw is excluded, and R/data-raw-helpers.R and R/lintr.R are kept; the second half of the output shows what the same names would do without anchors: a pattern data-raw or lintr matches anywhere in a path and would throw away the helper files as well.

# .Rbuildignore holds one Perl-style regular expression per line, matched
# case-insensitively against each path relative to the package root.
patterns <- c(
  "^LICENSE\\.md$", "^data-raw$", "^cran-comments\\.md$", "^\\.lintr$"
)
paths <- c(
  "DESCRIPTION", "LICENSE", "LICENSE.md", "license.MD", "data-raw",
  "data-raw/books.R", "R/data-raw-helpers.R", "cran-comments.md",
  ".lintr", "R/lintr.R"
)
is_ignored <- function(path, patterns) {
  hits <- vapply(patterns, grepl, logical(1L), x = path,
                 perl = TRUE, ignore.case = TRUE)
  any(hits)
}
ignored <- vapply(paths, is_ignored, logical(1L), patterns = patterns)
data.frame(path = paths, ignored = ignored, row.names = NULL)
#>                    path ignored
#> 1           DESCRIPTION   FALSE
#> 2               LICENSE   FALSE
#> 3            LICENSE.md    TRUE
#> 4            license.MD    TRUE
#> 5              data-raw    TRUE
#> 6      data-raw/books.R   FALSE
#> 7  R/data-raw-helpers.R   FALSE
#> 8      cran-comments.md    TRUE
#> 9                .lintr    TRUE
#> 10            R/lintr.R   FALSE

# The anchors matter. Without them a pattern matches anywhere in the path.
loose <- c("data-raw", "lintr")
vapply(paths, is_ignored, logical(1L), patterns = loose)
#>          DESCRIPTION              LICENSE           LICENSE.md
#>                FALSE                FALSE                FALSE
#>           license.MD             data-raw     data-raw/books.R
#>                FALSE                 TRUE                 TRUE
#> R/data-raw-helpers.R     cran-comments.md               .lintr
#>                 TRUE                FALSE                 TRUE
#>            R/lintr.R
#>                 TRUE

# "^data-raw$" ignores the directory; R CMD build then does not descend
# into it, so "data-raw/books.R" is not matched on its own and does not
# need to be.

Source: R documentation: grep, grepl and the other regular-expression functions

The build also leaves out, without being told, some directories and files: those of version-control systems and of editors, directories named check, chm or ending in .Rcheck, Old or old, files such as GNUMakefile and Read-and-delete-me, backup files ending in ~, .bak or .swp, and the tarballs of earlier builds of the same package (Writing R Extensions, "Building package tarballs"). usethis adds a line for you: usethis::use_build_ignore("notes.txt") appends the escaped, anchored ^notes\.txt$, as the section on reading the output of R CMD check shows. A related file, .Rinstignore, excludes files of inst/ from the installation, not from the bundle.

A small experiment on a copy of the package shows the three behaviours of hidden and ignored files at once. The first lines create, inside the package directory, a file .hidden at the top level, a directory inst/extra with two files, keep.txt and skip.tmp, and a .Rinstignore that holds the pattern \.tmp$. Then the commands run from the parent of the package: the bundle is built without the vignettes to keep the run short, the listing shows what ended up in it, the package is installed into a library directory lib, and R CMD check is run with its slow steps switched off.

cd shelf
mkdir -p inst/extra
echo a > inst/extra/keep.txt
echo b > inst/extra/skip.tmp
echo '\.tmp$' > .Rinstignore
echo x > .hidden
cd ..
R CMD build --no-build-vignettes shelf
tar tzf shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz | grep -e '/\.[A-Za-z]' -e extra
mkdir lib
R CMD INSTALL --library=lib shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz
ls lib/shelf/extra
R CMD check --no-manual --no-vignettes --no-tests --no-examples shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz

Source: R documentation: R CMD build and R CMD check

The bundle holds .hidden and .Rinstignore and both files of inst/extra, so the build did not apply .Rinstignore; the installation did, and installed only keep.txt; and the check reported the hidden file. The lines that are not the point (the build and installation logs, the platform header and the steps that passed) are left out, and so is the check’s final status: with --no-vignettes and --no-tests the check also warns about the vignettes that the build skipped, which has nothing to do with the experiment.

shelf/.Rinstignore
shelf/.hidden
shelf/inst/extra/
shelf/inst/extra/keep.txt
shelf/inst/extra/skip.tmp
[...]
keep.txt
[...]
* checking for hidden files and directories ... NOTE
Found the following hidden files and directories:
  .hidden
These were most likely included in error. See section ‘Package
structure’ in the ‘Writing R Extensions’ manual.

Source: Writing R Extensions: Package subdirectories

The DESCRIPTION file

DESCRIPTION is a plain text file in the format of a Debian control file: a field name, a colon, and a value, with continuation lines that start with a space or a tab. R reads it with read.dcf(), library() reads it before loading a package, R CMD INSTALL copies it into the installed package, and CRAN and every package manager read it to resolve dependencies. Field names are case-sensitive and all the ones R uses are capitalised. Here is the file of shelf exactly as the tools left it. The order of the fields is the order in which the tools added them (Depends is near the end because usethis::use_package() added it after the file existed), and the order has no meaning.

Package: shelf
Title: Tools for a Small Library Catalogue
Version: 0.1.0
Authors@R:
    person("Shelf", "Maintainers", , "maintainer@example.com", role = c("aut", "cre", "cph"))
Description: Cleans a small library catalogue and its loans table,
    validates ISBN-13 strings, and reports overdue loans and overdue rates
    by genre. Ships the example 'books' and 'loans' datasets used by the
    documentation.
License: MIT + file LICENSE
Config/roxygen2/version: 8.1.1
Encoding: UTF-8
Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE)
Suggests:
    knitr,
    rmarkdown,
    testthat (>= 3.0.0),
    withr
Config/testthat/edition: 3
Depends:
    R (>= 4.1.0)
VignetteBuilder: knitr
LazyData: true

Source: Writing R Extensions: The DESCRIPTION file

Writing R Extensions makes seven fields mandatory: Package, Version, License, Description, Title, Author and Maintainer. The last two can be generated from Authors@R and may be left out if that field is given, and CRAN requires Authors@R for a submission, so a modern file has Authors@R and not Author and Maintainer. Everything else is optional. The sections below take the fields in the order in which a new package needs them.

Field Written by What it does

Package, Title, Version, Description

usethis::create_package()

The name, a one-line title in title case, the version and a one-paragraph description.

Authors@R

create_package()

R code that builds a person object with names, e-mail addresses and roles.

License

usethis::use_mit_license()

A standard licence abbreviation, optionally with + file LICENSE.

Depends, Imports, Suggests, LinkingTo, Enhances

usethis::use_package() and the other use_* functions

The packages (and the version of R) that this package needs.

Encoding, LazyData, VignetteBuilder

create_package(), use_data() and use_vignette()

How the files are encoded, whether datasets load lazily, and which package builds the vignettes.

Config/testthat/edition, Config/roxygen2/version, Roxygen

use_testthat() and roxygen2

Settings of tools, kept in the file so that every contributor gets the same ones.

Collate, URL, BugReports, SystemRequirements, NeedsCompilation, Date, Language

You, roxygen2 or the build

Optional: file order, web addresses, external software, whether there is compiled code, a release date, the language of the documentation.

Package, Title and Description

The Package field is the name, and the rule is short and strict: only ASCII letters, numbers and dots, at least two characters, a letter first, and no dot at the end. A hyphen or an underscore is not allowed. usethis checks this before it creates anything, and its message names the rules; the first call below is that check.

# A new package with the defaults: the name is checked first.
tryCatch(
  usethis::create_package("~/my-package", open = FALSE),
  error = \(e) cat(conditionMessage(e), "\n")
)
#> ✖ "my-package" is not a valid package name. To be allowed on CRAN, it
#>   should:
#> • Contain only ASCII letters, numbers, and '.'.
#> • Have at least two characters.
#> • Start with a letter.
#> • Not end with '.'.

# A valid name creates the directory, DESCRIPTION and NAMESPACE.
usethis::create_package("~/tinyshelf", rstudio = FALSE, open = FALSE)
#> ✔ Creating '~/tinyshelf/'.
#> ✔ Setting active project to "~/tinyshelf".
#> ✔ Creating 'R/'.
#> ✔ Writing 'DESCRIPTION'.
#> Package: tinyshelf
#> Title: What the Package Does (One Line, Title Case)
#> Version: 0.0.0.9000
#> Authors@R (parsed):
#>     * First Last <first.last@example.com> [aut, cre]
#> Description: What the package does (one paragraph).
#> License: `use_mit_license()`, `use_gpl3_license()` or friends to pick a
#>     license
#> Config/roxygen2/version: 8.1.1
#> Encoding: UTF-8
#> Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE)
#> ✔ Writing 'NAMESPACE'.
#> ✔ Setting active project to "<no active project>".
usethis::proj_set("~/tinyshelf")
#> ✔ Setting active project to "~/tinyshelf".
list.files("~/tinyshelf", all.files = TRUE, no.. = TRUE)
#> [1] "DESCRIPTION" "NAMESPACE"   "R"

# A first function, a licence and the version bump for development.
usethis::use_r("squish")
#> ☐ Edit 'R/squish.R'.
usethis::use_mit_license("Shelf Maintainers")
#> ✔ Adding "MIT + file LICENSE" to 'License'.
#> ✔ Writing 'LICENSE'.
#> ✔ Writing 'LICENSE.md'.
#> ✔ Adding "^LICENSE\\.md$" to '.Rbuildignore'.
usethis::use_news_md(open = FALSE)
#> ✔ Writing 'NEWS.md'.
usethis::use_version("dev")
#> ✔ Adding "0.0.0.9001" to 'Version'.
readLines("~/tinyshelf/NEWS.md")
#> [1] "# tinyshelf (development version)" ""
#> [3] "* Initial CRAN submission."
unlink("~/tinyshelf", recursive = TRUE)

Source: usethis package documentation: create_package

The output after the error is what a package looks like straight after create_package() with no arguments: a DESCRIPTION with placeholders (Title: What the Package Does (One Line, Title Case), a made-up author, a version 0.0.0.9000 and a licence field that tells you to pick one), an empty NAMESPACE and an empty R/. The calls after it show the next three steps, each writing or editing a file: use_r() makes R/squish.R (the name goes with the function), use_mit_license() adds the licence, and use_news_md() adds a NEWS.md.

A package name is also a name in CRAN’s namespace of packages: The CRAN Repository Policy asks that a package be named in a way that does not conflict, irrespective of case, with any current or past CRAN package or any current Bioconductor package. The check that tests it is the incoming one that the section on R CMD check runs on shelf, which fails, for a reason that is the best illustration of the rule: a package called SHELF exists. The name is a decision to make before the first release, and Publishing to CRAN says what to do about it.

The Title is what package lists show. It is a short phrase in title case, with no markup, no continuation lines and no full stop at the end; it should not repeat the package name (it is nearly always displayed after it), and other packages and external software are written in single quotes, such as 'Rcpp' or 'GDAL'. Some listings truncate it at 65 characters, so the first 65 should carry the meaning. tools::toTitleCase() applies the capitalisation rules. The Description is a paragraph of complete sentences that says what the package does and why it is useful, aimed at everyone who might look for it. It should not start with "This package" or the package name, it uses single quotes for names of software and data (as shelf does for 'books' and 'loans'), double quotes for quotations, and angle brackets around URLs, as in https://www.r-project.org.

Version

The Version is a sequence of at least two, and usually three, non-negative integers separated by single . or - characters. It is not a decimal number, so 0.9 is less than 0.75 because 9 is less than 75, and 1.10 is later than 1.9. R represents such versions with numeric_version and, for package versions, its subclass package_version; getRversion() returns the same kind of object for R itself, and packageVersion() returns one for an installed package. The script shows what the class does.

# Version numbers are not decimals: they are sequences of integers.
v <- package_version(c("0.1.0", "0.1.0.9000", "0.9", "0.75", "1.0.0", "1.0-1"))
v
#> [1] ‘0.1.0’      ‘0.1.0.9000’ ‘0.9’        ‘0.75’       ‘1.0.0’
#> [6] ‘1.0.1’
class(v)
#> [1] "package_version" "numeric_version"
v[[3L]] < v[[4L]]
#> [1] TRUE
sort(v)
#> [1] ‘0.1.0’      ‘0.1.0.9000’ ‘0.9’        ‘0.75’       ‘1.0.0’
#> [6] ‘1.0.1’
max(v)
#> [1] ‘1.0.1’

# The pieces of a version.
x <- package_version("0.1.0.9000")
unlist(x)
#> [1]    0    1    0 9000
x$major
#> [1] 0
x$minor
#> [1] 1
x$patchlevel
#> [1] 0

# Comparisons accept a string on one side.
package_version("1.10.0") > "1.9.0"
#> [1] TRUE
numeric_version("1.10.0") > numeric_version("1.9.0")
#> [1] TRUE
as.numeric("1.10") > as.numeric("1.9")
#> [1] FALSE

# `-` and `.` are equivalent separators, and trailing zeros are not
# significant for comparison.
package_version("1.0-1") == package_version("1.0.1")
#> [1] TRUE
package_version("0.5") == package_version("0.5.0")
#> [1] TRUE
compareVersion("1.10.0", "1.9.0")
#> [1] 1

# What R itself is.
getRversion() >= "4.1.0"
#> [1] TRUE
getRversion() >= "4.7.0"
#> [1] FALSE
is.numeric_version(getRversion())
#> [1] TRUE
class(getRversion())
#> [1] "R_system_version" "package_version"  "numeric_version"

# A malformed version is an error.
tryCatch(package_version("1.0.beta"), error = \(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "invalid version specification ‘1.0.beta’"

# Installed packages report their version as a package_version.
packageVersion("stats") >= "4.1.0"
#> [1] TRUE
packageVersion("utils")
#> [1] ‘4.6.1’

# Leading zeros are dropped within a component: "0.01" is 0.1.
unlist(package_version("0.01"))
#> [1] 0 1

Source: R documentation: numeric_version, package_version and R_system_version

The comparisons in the middle of that output are the ones that matter for a package: package_version("1.10.0") > "1.9.0" is TRUE and the same comparison on decimals is FALSE, a string on one side is converted, - and . separate components in the same way, trailing zeros do not change the comparison, and getRversion() >= "4.1.0" is the idiom for code that depends on the R version. The last lines show that a leading zero is dropped inside a component ("0.01" is the version 0.1) and that a malformed version is an error.

Most packages use three components, major.minor.patch, plus a fourth component while they are in development. The convention, which comes from the community tooling and is not an R rule, is to give a development version a fourth component that starts at 9000: 0.1.0.9000 is later than the release 0.1.0 and earlier than the next release 0.1.1 or 0.2.0, so anybody who installs from the repository can tell a released version from a work in progress. usethis automates it with use_version(): the argument is "major", "minor", "patch" or "dev", and it also edits the heading of NEWS.md (and, in a package under Git, commits the change). The script below runs the whole sequence on a copy of shelf: a development version, a patch release, a minor release and a development version again.

# Version bumps with usethis, on a copy of the package.
desc_version <- \() read.dcf("DESCRIPTION", fields = "Version")[[1L]]
desc_version()
#> [1] "0.1.0"
usethis::use_version("dev")
#> ✔ Setting active project to
#>   "~/shelf".
#> ✔ Adding "0.1.0.9000" to 'Version'.
#> ✔ Adding new heading to 'NEWS.md'.
desc_version()
#> [1] "0.1.0.9000"
usethis::use_version("patch")
#> ✔ Adding "0.1.1" to 'Version'.
#> ✔ Replacing development heading in 'NEWS.md'.
desc_version()
#> [1] "0.1.1"
usethis::use_version("minor")
#> ✔ Adding "0.2.0" to 'Version'.
#> ✔ Adding new heading to 'NEWS.md'.
desc_version()
#> [1] "0.2.0"
usethis::use_version("dev")
#> ✔ Adding "0.2.0.9000" to 'Version'.
#> ✔ Adding new heading to 'NEWS.md'.
desc_version()
#> [1] "0.2.0.9000"
readLines("NEWS.md")
#>  [1] "# shelf (development version)"
#>  [2] ""
#>  [3] "# shelf 0.2.0"
#>  [4] ""
#>  [5] "# shelf 0.1.1"
#>  [6] ""
#>  [7] "# shelf 0.1.0"
#>  [8] ""
#>  [9] "* Initial version: the `book` class, `clean_books()`, `clean_loans()`,"
#> [10] "  `overdue_loans()`, `loan_summary()` and `loans_per_month()`, with the"
#> [11] "  `books` and `loans` datasets."

Source: usethis package documentation: use_version

The first use_version("dev") added the heading "shelf (development version)" to NEWS.md, the patch release replaced that heading with # shelf 0.1.1 (on use_version("patch") the heading of the development version becomes the heading of the release) and the next "dev" started a new development heading. The Version field is also what packageVersion("shelf") and citation("shelf") report, and the one place where the number must not be edited by hand is a release: CRAN requires the version to increase with every submission, and the release step of the CRAN page is where use_version() is used.

Authors@R and the person class

The Authors@R field is R code, evaluated when the package is built or installed, that creates an object of class person with person(), or several of them joined with c(). A person has given and family names, an e-mail address, one or more roles and a comment. The roles are codes from the MARC list of relators, and ?person suggests how to use them in packages: "aut" (author) for people who made substantial contributions and should appear in the citation, "cre" (creator) for the maintainer, "ctb" (contributor) for smaller contributions, "cph" (copyright holder, which has to be the legal name of a person or an institution), "fnd" (funder) for who paid for the work, and "com", "ctr", "dtc", "rev", "ths" and "trl" for compilers, contractors, data contributors, reviewers, thesis advisors and translators. No role is assumed: a person without a role is not listed as an author. The comment can hold an ORCID or a ROR identifier under the names ORCID and ROR, which print() and format() turn into links; the identifier in the script is the example iD that ORCID itself uses in its documentation.

# Authors@R is R code that builds a "person" object.
authors <- c(
  person("Shelf", "Maintainers", email = "maintainer@example.com",
         role = c("aut", "cre", "cph")),
  person("Ada", "Contributor", role = "ctb",
         comment = c(ORCID = "0000-0002-1825-0097")),
  person("Example Library Fund", role = "fnd")
)
authors
#> [1] "Shelf Maintainers <maintainer@example.com> [aut, cre, cph]"
#> [2] "Ada Contributor [ctb] (ORCID: <https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1825-0097>)"
#> [3] "Example Library Fund [fnd]"

# The pieces are available as fields.
authors$role
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "aut" "cre" "cph"
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "ctb"
#> [[3]]
#> [1] "fnd"
authors[[1L]]$email
#> [1] "maintainer@example.com"
authors[[2L]]$comment
#>                 ORCID
#> "0000-0002-1825-0097"

# R CMD build and R CMD INSTALL derive the Author and Maintainer fields:
format(authors, include = c("given", "family", "role"))
#> [1] "Shelf Maintainers [aut, cre, cph]" "Ada Contributor [ctb]"
#> [3] "Example Library Fund [fnd]"
cre <- Filter(\(p) "cre" %in% p$role, authors)
format(cre, include = c("given", "family", "email"),
       braces = list(email = c("<", ">")))
#> [1] "Shelf Maintainers <maintainer@example.com>"

Source: R documentation: person

R CMD build and R CMD INSTALL derive the plain Author and Maintainer fields from Authors@R, which is what the last two lines of the script format: Author: Shelf Maintainers [aut, cre, cph] and Maintainer: Shelf Maintainers <maintainer@example.com> are in the installed DESCRIPTION, as the inspection section shows. The cre person needs a valid e-mail address that will keep working for the life of the package, because that is where CRAN writes. The address of shelf is a placeholder, which is one more reason why the package cannot be submitted as it is.

License

Every package needs a License field, and without one it is not even legal for other people to distribute it. R wants the field in a standard form so that tools can tell whether a licence is "free or open source" (FOSS) and whether it restricts use. A licence is written as an abbreviation from R’s licence database, optionally with a version restriction, such as GPL (>= 3), LGPL (>= 2.1) or Apache License (== 2.0); as one of the standard short forms (GPL-2, GPL-3, LGPL-2, LGPL-2.1, LGPL-3, AGPL-3, Artistic-2.0, BSD_2_clause, BSD_3_clause and MIT); as file LICENSE, which refers to a file of the package; or as alternatives separated by a vertical bar. "Public domain" is not a valid licence, because it is not recognised everywhere. The script reads the database that ships with R and asks the internal helper that R CMD check uses to judge a few specifications.

# R keeps a database of recognised licences next to the standard texts.
db <- read.dcf(file.path(R.home("share"), "licenses", "license.db"))
nrow(db)
#> [1] 32
version <- ifelse(is.na(db[, "Version"]), "", paste0(" ", db[, "Version"]))
standard <- paste0(db[, "Abbrev"], version)
head(standard[!grepl("^NA", standard)], 14L)
#>  [1] "GPL 2"        "GPL 3"        "LGPL 2"       "LGPL 2.1"     "LGPL 3"
#>  [6] "AGPL 3"       "CeCILL 2"     "CeCILL 2.1"   "FreeBSD"      "MIT"
#> [11] "BSD_2_clause" "BSD_3_clause" "MPL 1.0"      "MPL 1.1"
sort(list.files(file.path(R.home("share"), "licenses"), pattern = "^[A-Z]"))
#>  [1] "AGPL-3"       "Apache-2.0"   "Artistic-2.0" "BSD_2_clause" "BSD_3_clause"
#>  [6] "CC0-1.0"      "GPL-2"        "GPL-3"        "LGPL-2"       "LGPL-2.1"
#> [11] "LGPL-3"       "MIT"

# `tools:::analyze_license()` is the internal helper that R CMD check uses
# to judge the License field; it is not a stable API, it is shown only to
# see what check sees.
specs <- c("MIT + file LICENSE", "GPL (>= 3)", "GPL-3 | file LICENSE",
           "Apache License (== 2.0)", "Public domain")
verdict <- lapply(specs, \(s) {
  a <- tools:::analyze_license(s)
  data.frame(License = s, canonical = a$is_canonical, FOSS = a$is_FOSS,
             restricts_use = a$restricts_use)
})
do.call(rbind, verdict)
#>                   License canonical FOSS restricts_use
#> 1      MIT + file LICENSE      TRUE TRUE         FALSE
#> 2              GPL (>= 3)      TRUE TRUE         FALSE
#> 3    GPL-3 | file LICENSE      TRUE TRUE         FALSE
#> 4 Apache License (== 2.0)      TRUE TRUE         FALSE
#> 5           Public domain     FALSE   NA            NA

Source: Writing R Extensions: Licensing

shelf uses MIT + file LICENSE. The MIT licence is a template: it needs a year and a copyright holder, and R’s convention is that a licence that needs additional information is written with + file LICENSE, where LICENSE is a small file with the two fields and nothing else. usethis::use_mit_license() wrote that file, the full licence text as LICENSE.md (which GitHub shows and the bundle does not need: ^LICENSE\.md$ went into .Rbuildignore), and the field. The file is two lines.

YEAR: 2026
COPYRIGHT HOLDER: shelf authors

Source: usethis package documentation: licenses

Writing R Extensions says that the copyright holder must be a real legal entity and not something vague such as the name of the package with "authors" added. use_mit_license() was called without a name, so it wrote shelf authors, which is acceptable for a demonstration and is the kind of thing the CRAN reviewers ask to change; pass your name or your organisation’s, as in use_mit_license("Shelf Maintainers"). The other functions of the same family write other licences: use_gpl_license(), use_agpl_license(), use_lgpl_license() and use_apache_license() (each with a version and an include_future argument that makes the licence "or any later version"), use_cc0_license() and use_ccby_license() for data packages, and use_proprietary_license() for code that is not to be shared. They save the standard text as LICENSE.md and add it to .Rbuildignore, because CRAN does not accept copies of the standard licences inside a package. Which licence to use is the author’s choice and a legal one; the rules of the CRAN policy are in Publishing to CRAN.

Depends, Imports, Suggests, LinkingTo and Enhances

A package declares what it needs in five fields that differ in what R does with the names.

Field What R does with the packages Use it for

Depends

Installs them and attaches them to the search path before attaching this package. Also the place to state the minimum version of R.

Packages the user must have attached to use yours, such as the packages whose functions your functions are extensions of, and R (>= x.y.z).

Imports

Installs them and loads their namespaces when this one is loaded, but does not attach them. The names they export are available to this package through NAMESPACE, or through ::.

Packages whose functions the code calls. The default home for dependencies.

Suggests

Does not install them by default. They are needed to run the tests, examples and vignettes, or for an optional feature.

Testing and documentation packages, packages used only conditionally (requireNamespace()).

LinkingTo

Makes their C and C++ header files available when this package’s compiled code is built.

Header-only or header-providing packages such as Rcpp.

Enhances

Nothing is installed. The package says that it adds support for objects or methods from these packages.

Rare: packages for whose objects you provide methods without needing them.

Source: Writing R Extensions: Package Dependencies

The rules in Writing R Extensions fit on a few lines. A package should be listed in only one of the fields. A package whose functions this one calls belongs in Imports; Depends is only for packages that have to be attached for the user’s benefit, and the manual says that the field should be used only rarely nowadays, because attaching a package changes the search path of everybody who loads yours (the Packages, Libraries and Namespaces page explains masking). Packages used to run examples, tests or vignettes belong in Suggests, which also lets checkers verify that everything needed for a full check is installed, and code that uses a suggested package must test for it first. Version requirements are written in parentheses with a comparison operator, testthat (>= 3.0.0); for Depends and Imports R checks them when the package is loaded, and for Suggests the code that uses the package is responsible for checking.

usethis::use_package() edits the right field, adds a version requirement when asked, and prints the advice that goes with the field. The script runs it on a copy of shelf, for an import, a suggestion, a LinkingTo entry and an import with a minimum version, and then reads the result back; the second half of the script shows what @include does to the Collate field, which is discussed with the other optional fields below. The messages print the path of the package, which is shortened here to ~/shelf.

# Declaring dependencies: use_package() edits the right field.
usethis::use_package("utils")
#> ✔ Setting active project to
#>   "~/shelf".
#> ✔ Adding utils to 'Imports' field in DESCRIPTION.
#> ☐ Refer to functions with `utils::fun()`.
usethis::use_package("stringr", "Suggests")
#> ✔ Adding stringr to 'Suggests' field in DESCRIPTION.
#> ☐ Use `requireNamespace("stringr", quietly = TRUE)` to test if stringr is
#>   installed.
#> ☐ Then directly refer to functions with `stringr::fun()`.
usethis::use_package("Rcpp", "LinkingTo")
#> ✔ Adding Rcpp to 'LinkingTo' field in DESCRIPTION.
#> Possible includes are:
#>   #include <Rcpp.h>
#>   #include <RcppCommon.h>
usethis::use_package("MASS", min_version = "7.3-60")
#> ✔ Adding MASS to 'Imports' field in DESCRIPTION.
#> ☐ Refer to functions with `MASS::fun()`.
fields <- c("Depends", "Imports", "Suggests", "LinkingTo")
desc <- read.dcf("DESCRIPTION", fields = fields)
cat(paste0(fields, ": ", gsub("\n", " ", desc[1L, ]), collapse = "\n"), "\n")
#> Depends: R (>= 4.1.0)
#> Imports: MASS (>= 7.3-60), utils
#> Suggests: knitr, rmarkdown, stringr, testthat (>= 3.0.0), withr
#> LinkingTo: Rcpp

# roxygen2 writes the Collate field when a file says it must come after
# another one with @include.
clean <- readLines("R/clean.R")
export_at <- grep("^#' @export$", clean)[[1L]]
clean <- append(clean, "#' @include isbn.R", after = export_at - 1L)
writeLines(clean, "R/clean.R")
roxygen2::roxygenise()
#> Updating collate directive in
#> '~/shelf/DESCRIPTION'
#> ℹ Loading shelf
#> shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
desc <- read.dcf("DESCRIPTION", fields = "Collate")
cat("Collate:", gsub("\n", " ", desc[[1L]]), "\n")
#> Collate: 'book.R' 'isbn.R' 'clean.R' 'data.R' 'loans.R' 'zzz.R'

Source: usethis package documentation: use_package

The advice that came with Suggests is the standard pattern for an optional dependency, and it is the one that Writing R Extensions recommends: test with requireNamespace("stringr", quietly = TRUE) and call the function as stringr::fun(). The manual explains why a require() call is not good practice in package code: it alters the search path for the rest of the session, and it relies on other packages not masking functions. For the same reason there is no library() call anywhere in the code of shelf.

The line Depends: R (>= 4.1.0) is the one that shelf cannot do without, and its story is a good example of how the checks work. R/isbn.R uses the function shorthand \(i), which was added in R 4.1.0 together with the native pipe |>. A package that uses either must say so, because on an older R the file does not even parse. When the field is missing, R CMD build notices it and adds the dependency itself, with a warning that says what it saw. The next block runs R CMD build on a copy of shelf whose Depends lines were deleted.

R CMD build shelf

Source: R documentation: R CMD build and R CMD check

* checking for file ‘shelf/DESCRIPTION’ ... OK
* preparing ‘shelf’:
* checking DESCRIPTION meta-information ... OK
* installing the package (it is needed to build vignettes)
* creating vignettes ... OK
* checking for LF line-endings in source and make files and shell scripts
* checking for empty or unneeded directories
  NB: this package now depends on R (>= 3.5.0)
  WARNING: Added dependency on R >= 3.5.0 because serialized objects in
  serialize/load version 3 cannot be read in older versions of R.
  File(s) containing such objects:
    ‘shelf/R/sysdata.rda’ ‘shelf/data/books.rda’ ‘shelf/data/loans.rda’
  NB: this package now depends on R (>= 4.1.0)
  WARNING: Added dependency on R >= 4.1.0 because package code uses the
  pipe |> or function shorthand \(...) syntax added in R 4.1.0.
  File(s) using such syntax:
    ‘isbn.R’
* building ‘shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz’

Source: Writing R Extensions: Package Dependencies

There are two warnings in that output, both for the same family of reasons. The second is the one for the missing field: the build found isbn.R using syntax added in R 4.1.0 and added R (>= 4.1.0) to the DESCRIPTION of the bundle. The first is the same mechanism applied to the data files: usethis::use_data() saves with serialization version 3, which R 3.5.0 introduced (the NEWS of R 3.6.0 made it the default for save()), and an older R cannot read such a file, so the build added R (>= 3.5.0) too. Writing Depends: R (>= 4.1.0) in the source makes both messages go away, because 4.1.0 is later than 3.5.0. A build that adds a dependency has also changed the DESCRIPTION of the bundle, so that the bundle and the source no longer agree, which is one more reason to write the field yourself. The manual recommends a minimum version of R with a patch level of zero: a package that requires a patch release makes every package that depends on it unusable on the earlier patch releases of the same series.

Two more fields belong with the dependencies. Additional_repositories is a comma-separated list of repository URLs where packages named in the other fields can be found; R CMD check uses it to check that they can be found, at least as source packages. Remotes is not an R field: it belongs to the community tools (remotes, pak, devtools) and says where to install a dependency that is not on CRAN, which is why a package that is to go to CRAN cannot depend on one (usethis::use_dev_package() writes it). Dependencies outside R, such as a command-line program or a system library, are listed in SystemRequirements, in words, because R cannot install them.

Two ways of getting the dependency fields wrong stop the installation, and both have a short, exact message. A package that needs a newer R than the one in use, and a package whose dependency is not installed, are reported by R CMD INSTALL and nothing is installed. The two copies of shelf below had R (>= 9.0.0) in Depends and notinstalledpkg in Imports.

R CMD INSTALL --library=lib shelf

Source: R documentation: INSTALL

ERROR: this R is version 4.6.1, package 'shelf' requires R >= 9.0.0
ERROR: dependency ‘notinstalledpkg’ is not available for package ‘shelf’
Perhaps try a variation of:
install.packages('notinstalledpkg')

Source: R Installation and Administration: Installing packages

The first line came from the first copy and the other three from the second; the second copy also printed a line that says it removed the half-installed package from the library, which is left out. In both cases the installation fails with a non-zero status and the library is left as it was.

The other fields

The remaining fields are optional. The ones that matter most are these.

Field What it says

Encoding

The encoding of the DESCRIPTION, the R and NAMESPACE files and, by default, of the Rd files. R wants it only when something is not ASCII, and Writing R Extensions advises not to specify an encoding unless one is needed, because only latin1 and UTF-8 are portable. usethis writes Encoding: UTF-8 into every new package, and roxygen2 and the documentation tools assume it.

LazyData

A logical: whether the datasets in data/ are lazy-loaded, so that books is visible when the package is attached without calling data(). use_data() set it to true, and R CMD check verifies it (the step "checking LazyData").

VignetteBuilder

The package or packages that build the vignettes: knitr for R Markdown vignettes. Together with Suggests: knitr, rmarkdown, which use_vignette() also added.

Config/testthat/edition

3 selects testthat’s third edition (stricter, waldo-based comparisons and snapshot defaults). Fields with the prefix Config/ are a convention that keeps the settings of a tool in the DESCRIPTION; R ignores them.

Config/roxygen2/version

The version of roxygen2 that last documented the package. roxygen2 8.0.0 and later store it here and no longer write RoxygenNote; see below.

Roxygen or Config/roxygen2/markdown

The options of roxygen2 for the package: Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE) turns on Markdown in the comments. See below.

URL, BugReports

Where the package lives and where to report problems. Each may be a list of URLs, converted into links on CRAN. shelf has neither: R CMD check --as-cran checks that URLs exist, and a placeholder address was reported as not found.

SystemRequirements

Dependencies outside R, in words: "GNU make", "libxml2 (>= 2.9)", a C++ standard.

NeedsCompilation

yes or no: whether the package has code to compile. The build and the repository set it, and a package with a src/ directory is assumed to need compilation. (The installed shelf has NeedsCompilation: no.)

Collate

The order in which the R files are read, if the default alphabetical order is not right. If present, it must list every file.

Date, Language, Copyright

A release date in ISO 8601 form (package.skeleton() adds today’s date, and many authors prefer not to carry a date that goes stale), the IETF language tag if the documentation is not English, and the copyright holders when they are not the authors.

ByteCompile, KeepSource, BuildVignettes, StagedInstall

Switches for the tools: byte-compile on installation (the default), keep source references, build vignettes in R CMD build, and the staged installation that has been the default since R 3.6.0.

Type

Package, the default. The other type recognised, Frontend, is a rare mechanism for adding GUI front-ends.

Source: Writing R Extensions: The DESCRIPTION file

The roxygen2 fields changed with roxygen2 8.0.0 (2026-05-01), which is the series installed here (8.1.1). Its NEWS says that the options can now be set in Config/roxygen2/ fields, so Config/roxygen2/markdown: TRUE replaces Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE) and the old field is still supported, and that the version is now stored in Config/roxygen2/version instead of RoxygenNote. usethis 3.2.2 still writes Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE) for a new package, which is why the shelf file has the old field next to the new version field. A package last documented with roxygen2 7.x has RoxygenNote; the first document() with roxygen2 8 migrates it, as the first of the two scripts below shows (the second field is left as it is), and the second script shows that the new Config/roxygen2/markdown form gives the same help pages: all the Rd files have the same checksums.

# A package last documented with roxygen2 7.x records RoxygenNote.
desc <- readLines("DESCRIPTION")
desc[desc == "Config/roxygen2/version: 8.1.1"] <- "RoxygenNote: 7.3.2"
writeLines(desc, "DESCRIPTION")
grep("oxygen", readLines("DESCRIPTION"), value = TRUE)
#> [1] "RoxygenNote: 7.3.2"             "Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE)"

# The first document() with roxygen2 8.x migrates the field.
roxygen2::roxygenise()
#> ℹ Setting Config/roxygen2/version to "8.1.1"
#> ℹ Loading shelf
#> shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
grep("oxygen", readLines("DESCRIPTION"), value = TRUE)
#> [1] "Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE)" "Config/roxygen2/version: 8.1.1"

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: NEWS

# roxygen2 8.x reads its options from Config/roxygen2/* fields as well.
desc <- readLines("DESCRIPTION")
old <- "Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE)"
desc[desc == old] <- "Config/roxygen2/markdown: TRUE"
writeLines(desc, "DESCRIPTION")
grep("oxygen", readLines("DESCRIPTION"), value = TRUE)
#> [1] "Config/roxygen2/version: 8.1.1" "Config/roxygen2/markdown: TRUE"

before <- tools::md5sum(list.files("man", full.names = TRUE))
roxygen2::roxygenise()
#> ℹ Loading shelf
#> shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
after <- tools::md5sum(list.files("man", full.names = TRUE))
identical(before, after)
#> [1] TRUE

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: NEWS

The Collate field is the one where hand-editing is most error-prone, so roxygen2 maintains it from @include tags. Without a tag there is no Collate field; with the line #' @include isbn.R in the comment block of clean_books() the field appeared in the script above (for the dependency copy) and listed every file of R/ with isbn.R placed before clean.R. The @include tag says that the current file needs the other one to be read first.

What the tools add

The DESCRIPTION of an installed package is not the file you wrote. The build and the installation add fields, and Writing R Extensions says that a source package should not have them itself: Packaged (who built the bundle and when), Author and Maintainer (derived from Authors@R), NeedsCompilation and, on installation, Built (the version of R, the platform and the date). The list of field names of the installed shelf is printed by names(packageDescription("shelf")), in the inspection section below.

The NAMESPACE file

A namespace is the part of a package that decides which of its names the world sees and which names it borrows from other packages. Without one, every function a package defines would be dumped into the user’s search path, masking what was already there. With one, a package exports a chosen few, keeps the rest private, and states precisely what it imports. Writing R Extensions describes the mechanism: the NAMESPACE file at the top of the package holds directives for exports, imports, S3 method registration and shared objects, and although the file looks like R code (and may have R-style comments) it is not processed as R code, apart from a very simple conditional on if statements. Loading a package loads its namespace, and attaching it puts only the exports on the search path. Two properties follow. Namespaces are sealed once loaded, so the bindings of a package cannot be changed from outside, and a function’s free variables are looked up in a fixed order: first the namespace itself, then the imports, then the base namespace, and only then the global environment and the rest of the search path.

The NAMESPACE of shelf was written by roxygen2, from the @export tags above the functions, the first time document() ran. It is a short file and it is complete.

# Generated by roxygen2: do not edit by hand

S3method(format,book)
S3method(print,book)
S3method(print,summary.book)
S3method(summary,book)
export(book)
export(clean_books)
export(clean_loans)
export(is_valid_isbn13)
export(loan_summary)
export(loans_per_month)
export(new_book)
export(normalise_isbn)
export(overdue_loans)
export(validate_book)

Source: Writing R Extensions: Package namespaces

It has two kinds of line. export(book) makes the function book() available to library(shelf) and to shelf::book. S3method(print, book) registers the function print.book() as the print method for class book, so print(b) dispatches to it. The function itself, print.book, is not exported and does not need to be, which is the point of registration: the generic print finds the method in a table that library() fills, not by searching for a name. All four methods of the book class are registered this way, and the print method of summary.book is too. The script asks the loaded namespace what it exposes.

# What a namespace exposes: the exports, and everything else.
ns <- asNamespace("shelf")
exports <- getNamespaceExports("shelf")
length(exports)
#> [1] 10
"squish" %in% exports
#> [1] FALSE
"squish" %in% ls(ns)
#> [1] TRUE

# An internal function is not reachable from outside by name ...
exists("squish")
#> [1] FALSE
tryCatch(shelf::squish("x"), error = \(e) conditionMessage(e))
#> [1] "'squish' is not an exported object from 'namespace:shelf'"
# ... but `:::` reaches it, which is fine in a test and wrong in other code.
shelf:::squish("  two   words  ")
#> [1] "two words"

# Inside the package, a name is looked up in the namespace, then in the
# imports, then in the base namespace, then on the search path.
environmentName(ns)
#> [1] "shelf"
environmentName(parent.env(ns))
#> [1] "imports:shelf"
environmentName(parent.env(parent.env(ns)))
#> [1] "base"
environmentName(parent.env(parent.env(parent.env(ns))))
#> [1] "R_GlobalEnv"

Source: R documentation: getNamespace, getNamespaceExports and the other namespace reflection functions

Ten functions are exported and everything else is private: squish(), shelf_today(), the two hooks, the S3 methods, and isbn_weights, which lives in R/sysdata.rda. The error message is the one a user sees when they try to call an internal function with ::, and ::: goes round the barrier. Using ::: on another package’s internals is "generally not recommended" in the words of the manual, because the author may rename or remove an unexported object in a routine release. The last four lines show the lookup chain that makes the namespace useful: the namespace shelf, its imports environment (here empty, because shelf imports nothing), the base namespace, and then the global environment, which is where the search path starts.

The directives

NAMESPACE has a small vocabulary. The table gives each directive with the roxygen2 tag that generates it, so a package maintained with roxygen2 never edits the file by hand.

Directive What it does roxygen2 tag

export(f, g)

Exports the named objects. Names may be quoted, and must be for reserved words and non-syntactic names.

@export

exportPattern("^api_")

Exports every object whose name matches a POSIX extended regular expression. Writing R Extensions says it is better to list the exports, or to use narrow groups, than a broad pattern such as ^[^.].

@exportPattern

S3method(print, book)

Registers the method for dispatch without exporting it. A third argument names a function with a different name. Since R 3.6.0 S3method(pkg::gen, cls) delays the registration until the namespace of pkg is loaded.

@export on the method, or @exportS3Method

import(pkg)

Imports every exported name of pkg. import(pkg, except = c(a, b)) leaves some out.

@import

importFrom(pkg, f, g)

Imports only the named objects. Writing R Extensions recommends it over import for packages with more than a dozen exports and for packages written by others.

@importFrom pkg f g

useDynLib(pkg, .registration = TRUE)

Loads the shared object pkg after the R code has been loaded and before .onLoad() runs, and defines R variables for the registered native routines.

@useDynLib pkg, .registration = TRUE

exportClasses©, exportMethods(g)

S4: exports the class and the methods of the generic. Also exportClassPattern().

@exportClass, @exportMethod

importClassesFrom(pkg, C), importMethodsFrom(pkg, g)

S4: imports classes and methods.

@importClassesFrom, @importMethodsFrom

if (getRversion() >= "3.6.0") S3method(pkg::gen, cls)

A simple conditional on a condition such as getRversion(), around any directive.

@rawNamespace, for any line that no other tag produces.

Source: Writing R Extensions: Specifying imports and exports

The script below writes a NAMESPACE with one of each directive and asks parseNamespaceFile(), the function that loadNamespace() uses, what it understood. It is a way to see the data structure behind the file: the exports are a character vector, the S3 methods a matrix of generic and class, the imports a list in which a bare name means "all" and a pair means "only these", and the dynamic library is a name.

# A NAMESPACE file looks like R code, but it is parsed with
# parseNamespaceFile(), which understands a fixed set of directives.
pkg <- file.path(tempdir(), "demopkg")
dir.create(pkg)
writeLines(c(
  "# every directive in one file",
  "export(f, g)",
  "exportPattern(\"^api_\")",
  "S3method(print, demo)",
  "S3method(format, demo)",
  "import(stats)",
  "importFrom(utils, head, tail)",
  "importFrom(tools, file_ext)",
  "exportClasses(Shelf)",
  "exportMethods(show)",
  "importClassesFrom(methods, ANY)",
  "useDynLib(demopkg, .registration = TRUE)"
), file.path(pkg, "NAMESPACE"))

ns <- parseNamespaceFile("demopkg", tempdir())
names(ns)
#>  [1] "imports"             "exports"             "exportPatterns"
#>  [4] "importClasses"       "importMethods"       "exportClasses"
#>  [7] "exportMethods"       "exportClassPatterns" "dynlibs"
#> [10] "nativeRoutines"      "S3methods"
ns$exports
#> [1] "f" "g"
ns$exportPatterns
#> [1] "^api_"
ns$S3methods[, 1:2]
#>      [,1]     [,2]
#> [1,] "print"  "demo"
#> [2,] "format" "demo"
str(ns$imports)
#> List of 3
#>  $ : chr "stats"
#>  $ :List of 2
#>   ..$ : chr "utils"
#>   ..$ : chr [1:2] "head" "tail"
#>  $ :List of 2
#>   ..$ : chr "tools"
#>   ..$ : chr "file_ext"
ns$exportClasses
#> [1] "Shelf"
ns$exportMethods
#> [1] "show"
ns$dynlibs
#>
#> "demopkg"
unlink(pkg, recursive = TRUE)

Source: R documentation: asNamespace, parseNamespaceFile and the internal namespace functions

The directives are the same in every package, and writing them is the part that roxygen2 does. The tags themselves are listed in Documentation with Rd, roxygen2 and Vignettes. The mapping above is enough to read a NAMESPACE and to predict what a tag will produce.

Importing from other packages

A package that uses functions of another package has three ways to say so, and they differ in what they cost. importFrom(pkg, f) in NAMESPACE, made by @importFrom pkg f, puts f in the imports environment, so the code calls f() plainly and the NAMESPACE records the dependency. pkg::f() in the code names the package at each call, loads but does not attach pkg when evaluated, and is slightly slower than a formal import; Writing R Extensions notes that it also loses the advantage of recording dependencies in NAMESPACE, but they still have to be recorded in DESCRIPTION. A fully qualified call is the only way to use two functions of the same name from different packages. The third, import(pkg), takes everything and risks name clashes with the package’s own functions, and the manual advises against it for large packages. Whichever way is used, the package must be listed in Imports (or Suggests for a conditional use), and R CMD check verifies it: the real warning for an undeclared jsonlite::toJSON() is in the section on check messages below.

The rule that has no exception is that package code does not call library() or require() to get at a function. Both attach a package, which changes the search path of the user’s whole session as a side effect of calling your function, and both fail in an uncontrolled way when the package is missing (library() stops, require() returns FALSE with a warning, and code that ignores the result fails later). For a package listed in Depends the call is unnecessary because it is already attached; for a package in Imports, :: or a formal import is the tool; and for a package in Suggests, requireNamespace("pkg", quietly = TRUE) followed by pkg::fun() tests for it without attaching anything. R CMD check reports a library() call in package code, as the real run below shows.

Generating the file

devtools::document() calls roxygen2::roxygenise(), which writes the NAMESPACE and the Rd files. roxygen2 does not trust a file that it did not make: the first line of the shelf file is "Generated by roxygen2: do not edit by hand", and a NAMESPACE without that line is left alone. The script writes a two-line hand-made file into a copy of the package and runs roxygen2, which skips the file and says why.

# A NAMESPACE written by hand (no "Generated by roxygen2" first line) is
# not overwritten by roxygen2.
writeLines(c("export(book)", "S3method(print, book)"), "NAMESPACE")
readLines("NAMESPACE")
#> [1] "export(book)"          "S3method(print, book)"
roxygen2::roxygenise()
#> ℹ Loading shelf
#> shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
#> ✖ Skipping NAMESPACE
#>   (<file://~/shelf/NAMESPACE>)
#> ℹ It already exists and was not generated by roxygen2.
readLines("NAMESPACE")
#> [1] "export(book)"          "S3method(print, book)"

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: Managing imports and exports

Hand-written NAMESPACE files are the way older tutorials work, and they were the only way until roxygen2 existed. They still work, and a package that already has one can keep it. What a new package gains from the generator is that the file can no longer disagree with the code: an exported function that is renamed has its @export tag in the same block, so the renaming is made once.

A package with no NAMESPACE file

Since R 2.14.0 every package has a namespace, and a package whose author wrote none gets one made for it. A copy of shelf with its NAMESPACE deleted shows the result: R CMD build says that it created a default file, the file is in the bundle, and the check then notices the consequence. The first command of the script removes the file, and tar xzOf prints the file from the tarball to the terminal.

rm shelf/NAMESPACE
R CMD build --no-build-vignettes shelf
tar xzOf shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz shelf/NAMESPACE
R CMD check --no-manual --no-vignettes --no-tests --no-examples shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz

Source: Writing R Extensions: Package namespaces

* creating default NAMESPACE file
* building ‘shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz’

# Default NAMESPACE created by R
# Remove the previous line if you edit this file

# Export all names
exportPattern("^[^.]")
[...]
* checking for missing documentation entries ... WARNING
Undocumented code objects:
  ‘isbn_weights’ ‘shelf_today’ ‘squish’
All user-level objects in a package should have documentation entries.
See chapter ‘Writing R documentation files’ in the ‘Writing R
Extensions’ manual.

Source: Writing R Extensions: Package namespaces

The default file exports every object whose name does not start with a dot. Since R 4.4.0 that is the pattern that the manual recommends (R NEWS: Changes in R 4.4.0: before it, R CMD build exported everything). It is why the check, in the second part of the output, reports isbn_weights, shelf_today and squish as undocumented code objects: they are the internal helpers, and without a NAMESPACE of their own they became part of the public interface. The run used --no-vignettes and the two other switches of the earlier experiment to keep it short, and the warnings about vignettes that it also printed are left out because they have nothing to do with the namespace. The lesson is that a default namespace is a stop-gap: a package that is meant to be used by other people has a NAMESPACE that lists what it exports.

Load hooks, options and start-up messages

Four hooks let a package run code when its namespace is loaded, attached, detached and unloaded. They are ordinary functions with fixed names, defined in the package and not exported (except for one, below), and R calls them at the right moment. The package shelf has two, in the file R/zzz.R, whose name makes it sort last, a convention that keeps the hooks out of the way. Here is the file, a package source like the others.

.onLoad <- function(libname, pkgname) {
  op <- options()
  op_shelf <- list(shelf.loan_days = 21L)
  to_set <- !(names(op_shelf) %in% names(op))
  if (any(to_set)) {
    options(op_shelf[to_set])
  }
  invisible()
}

.onAttach <- function(libname, pkgname) {
  packageStartupMessage(
    "shelf ", utils::packageVersion("shelf"),
    ": loan period is ", getOption("shelf.loan_days"), " days"
  )
}

Source: R documentation: .onLoad, .onAttach and the other hooks

.onLoad() runs when the namespace is loaded, and it is where the package sets its options. The idiom here is the standard one: collect the package’s options with their defaults in a list, find which of them the user has not already set, and set only those. A user who put options(shelf.loan_days = 14L) in their .Rprofile keeps 14, because the hook only fills in what is missing. .onAttach() runs when library() attaches the package, and it is where the start-up banner belongs. It uses packageStartupMessage(), which is a message() with a class that suppressPackageStartupMessages() recognises, so a script that does not want the banner can silence it without silencing real messages, and so can R CMD check: one of its steps is "checking whether startup messages can be suppressed". The script shows the whole story with the installed package: the namespace is loaded without a message, the banner appears only on library(), it can be silenced, and a user’s own setting wins.

# The scratch library holds the built shelf 0.1.0 (R_LIBS points to it).
# Loading the namespace runs .onLoad(), which sets the package option.
isNamespaceLoaded("shelf")
#> [1] FALSE
is.null(getOption("shelf.loan_days"))
#> [1] TRUE
requireNamespace("shelf", quietly = TRUE)
isNamespaceLoaded("shelf")
#> [1] TRUE
getOption("shelf.loan_days")
#> [1] 21
"package:shelf" %in% search()
#> [1] FALSE
shelf::normalise_isbn("978-0-00-100010-0")
#> [1] "9780001000100"

# library() attaches the package; .onAttach() prints the start-up message.
library(shelf)
#> shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
"package:shelf" %in% search()
#> [1] TRUE

# The message is a condition, so it can be silenced.
detach("package:shelf")
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(shelf))

# A user's own setting wins: .onLoad() only fills in what is unset.
detach("package:shelf", unload = TRUE)
options(shelf.loan_days = 14L)
library(shelf)
#> shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 14 days
getOption("shelf.loan_days")
#> [1] 14

Source: R documentation: message, packageStartupMessage and suppressPackageStartupMessages

Four lessons are packed in that output. Loading a namespace (here with requireNamespace(), and the same would hold for shelf::normalise_isbn()) runs .onLoad() and not .onAttach(): the option was set to 21 and package:shelf is not on the search path. library() runs .onAttach(), which printed the version and the loan period. A message created by packageStartupMessage() disappears under suppressPackageStartupMessages(). And the option of the user, set before library(), survived: .onLoad() saw shelf.loan_days already in options() and left it.

The four hooks in full, with the times at which R calls them and what each should be used for, are in the table.

Hook Called Use it for

.onLoad(libname, pkgname)

After the code is loaded, before the namespace is sealed and its exports processed. Runs for library(), loadNamespace() and ::.

Setting options, initialising state of the namespace, loading compiled code if there is no useDynLib directive. It must not assume that any package but base is attached, and must not attach one.

.onAttach(libname, pkgname)

When library() or attachNamespace() attaches the package, before the package environment is sealed.

A start-up banner (through packageStartupMessage()), and nothing else: most packages do not need it.

.onDetach(libpath) or an exported .Last.lib(libpath)

When the package is detached. Only one runs: .onDetach if the namespace has it, otherwise the exported .Last.lib.

Undoing what .onAttach() did. Should be written defensively, because it may be called even if .onAttach() failed.

.onUnload(libpath)

Before the namespace is unloaded by unloadNamespace() (and so by detach(unload = TRUE)).

Unloading compiled code with library.dynam.unload(). Not in .Last.lib or .onDetach.

Source: Writing R Extensions: Load hooks

A package of five lines can demonstrate the order, and the next script builds three such packages in a temporary library. The first, hooky, defines .onLoad, .onAttach, .onDetach and .onUnload, each printing a line with cat() (a real package would not print anything, and would use packageStartupMessage() for the banner). The second, lasty, defines only an exported .Last.lib, and the third, both, defines .onDetach and an exported .Last.lib. The script loads, attaches, detaches (twice) and unloads the first and prints the order in which the hooks ran, then attaches and detaches the other two.

# Build tiny packages whose hooks announce themselves, install them into a
# temporary library and watch the order in which the hooks run. (A real
# package uses packageStartupMessage(); cat() keeps the output ordered here.)
make_package <- function(name, exports, code) {
  src <- file.path(tempdir(), name)
