  dir.create(file.path(src, "R"), recursive = TRUE)
  writeLines(c(
    paste("Package:", name), "Version: 0.0.1", "Title: Announce Load Hooks",
    "Description: Prints a line when each load hook runs.",
    "License: MIT + file LICENSE", "Encoding: UTF-8"
  ), file.path(src, "DESCRIPTION"))
  writeLines(c("YEAR: 2026", "COPYRIGHT HOLDER: hook authors"),
             file.path(src, "LICENSE"))
  writeLines(exports, file.path(src, "NAMESPACE"))
  writeLines(code, file.path(src, "R", "hooks.R"))
  install.packages(src, repos = NULL, type = "source", lib = lib, quiet = TRUE)
}
lib <- file.path(tempdir(), "lib")
dir.create(lib)

make_package("hooky", "export(hello)", c(
  "hello <- function() \"hello\"",
  paste(".onLoad <- function(libname, pkgname)",
        "cat(\"  .onLoad   \", pkgname, \"\\n\")"),
  paste(".onAttach <- function(libname, pkgname)",
        "cat(\"  .onAttach \", pkgname, \"\\n\")"),
  ".onDetach <- function(libpath) cat(\"  .onDetach\\n\")",
  ".onUnload <- function(libpath) cat(\"  .onUnload\\n\")"
))
# The older hook: .Last.lib must be exported to be called.
make_package("lasty", "export(.Last.lib)", c(
  ".Last.lib <- function(libpath) cat(\"  .Last.lib\\n\")"
))
# With both, only .onDetach runs.
make_package("both", "export(.Last.lib)", c(
  ".onDetach <- function(libpath) cat(\"  .onDetach\\n\")",
  ".Last.lib <- function(libpath) cat(\"  .Last.lib\\n\")"
))
.libPaths(c(lib, .libPaths()))

cat("loadNamespace('hooky')\n")
#> loadNamespace('hooky')
invisible(loadNamespace("hooky"))
#>   .onLoad    hooky
cat("library(hooky)\n")
#> library(hooky)
library(hooky) # nolint: object_usage_linter.
#>   .onAttach  hooky
cat("detach('package:hooky')\n")
#> detach('package:hooky')
detach("package:hooky")
#>   .onDetach
cat("library(hooky) again\n")
#> library(hooky) again
library(hooky) # nolint: object_usage_linter.
#>   .onAttach  hooky
cat("detach('package:hooky', unload = TRUE)\n")
#> detach('package:hooky', unload = TRUE)
detach("package:hooky", unload = TRUE)
#>   .onDetach
#>   .onUnload
isNamespaceLoaded("hooky")
#> [1] FALSE
cat("hooky::hello()\n")
#> hooky::hello()
hooky::hello()
#>   .onLoad    hooky
#> [1] "hello"
unloadNamespace("hooky")
#>   .onUnload

cat("library(lasty); detach('package:lasty')\n")
#> library(lasty); detach('package:lasty')
library(lasty) # nolint: object_usage_linter.
detach("package:lasty")
#>   .Last.lib

cat("library(both); detach('package:both')\n")
#> library(both); detach('package:both')
library(both) # nolint: object_usage_linter.
detach("package:both")
#>   .onDetach
unlink(c(file.path(tempdir(), c("hooky", "lasty", "both")), lib),
       recursive = TRUE)

Source: R documentation: .onLoad, .onAttach and the other hooks

What the output shows is easy to get wrong in a package, and Writing R Extensions lists the usual mistakes. A namespace can be loaded without being attached (loadNamespace() ran .onLoad only). A package can be detached and attached again while its namespace stays loaded, so .onAttach ran twice and .onLoad once. detach(unload = TRUE) ran .onDetach first and then .onUnload, and the unloaded namespace was loaded again, with .onLoad, by the next hooky::hello(). Last, the two ways of writing a detach hook: .onDetach is in the namespace and is not exported, and the older .Last.lib has to be exported, and a package that defines both, like both, got only .onDetach in R 4.6.1: the help page says that the hook is called if .onDetach is in the namespace or .Last.lib is exported, and the output shows which of the two wins. People forget to export .Last.lib, which is why lasty has export(.Last.lib) in its NAMESPACE.

The rules of good practice in the help page are worth knowing by heart. A package should load silently. Any message that must be shown belongs in .onAttach() and goes through packageStartupMessage(). Hooks must not call library() or require(): a dependency is declared in Depends, or imported, and the namespace must not change the search path. They must not call installed.packages(), which is slow and can fail while another installation is running. Compiled code is loaded in .onLoad() (or by useDynLib) and unloaded in .onUnload() and nowhere else. And Writing R Extensions adds a warning about anything that depends on whether a suggested package is available: top-level code, .onLoad() functions and S4 class definitions run at installation time, and a reference to the namespace of a suggested package can be captured in the installed package, where it may be missing later.

Data in packages

A package can carry data in three places, and they have three different purposes. Which one to use is the first decision, and the table makes it.

Where What it is How users and code reach it

data/*.rda

Datasets for the user: books and loans. Written by usethis::use_data(). Documented in R/data.R.

data("books", package = "shelf"), or, because LazyData: true, plain books once the package is attached, and shelf::books without attaching.

R/sysdata.rda

Objects for the package itself, such as lookup tables: isbn_weights. Written by usethis::use_data(internal = TRUE). Not documented.

By name from the package’s own functions. Not visible to users, and not exported.

inst/extdata/

Raw files that the package reads or demonstrates, such as a CSV file.

system.file("extdata", "books.csv", package = "shelf").

Source: Writing R Extensions: Data in packages

The data directory

The data/ directory is for data files that are to be available through data() or, if the LazyData field is true, as lazy-loaded objects that exist as soon as the package is attached. A data file is one of three kinds, recognised by its extension: R code (.R), a table (.tab, .txt or .csv, read in the formats that ?data describes, noting that .csv here is not the standard CSV), or an image written by save() (.rda or .RData). Writing R Extensions says that data/ should not be used for other data files that the package needs, for which the convention is inst/extdata, and that an R file there should be self-sufficient and silent, not attaching packages. An .rda file is the usual choice: it keeps the classes, attributes and Date columns exactly (loans$loan_date is a Date, which a CSV could not guarantee), and it is compact.

The tool that writes the files is usethis::use_data(), one object per file, with compress = "bzip2" and version = 3 as the defaults (the serialization version that only R 3.5.0 and later can read, which is why the build added a dependency on R in the real run earlier). The tool that records how the data were made is the data-raw/ directory, which usethis creates with use_data_raw(): the script in it is the recipe, the CSV files next to it are the raw material, and .Rbuildignore keeps them out of the bundle. The step-by-step section shows the shelf script and what it printed. For the installed package the data/ directory holds a lazy-load database, which is the reason books costs nothing until it is used.

How the files were saved can be checked with tools::checkRdaFiles(), which reports the size, whether it is ASCII, the compression and the serialization version, and tools::resaveRdaFiles() re-saves a file with a better compression. R CMD check also inspects data files: the steps "checking contents of ‘data’ directory", "checking data for non-ASCII characters", "checking LazyData" and "checking data for ASCII and uncompressed saves" appear in the log. The same script loads the files into scratch environments and shows what each holds: data/ has the two datasets and R/sysdata.rda the one internal object.

# How the data files of the package were saved.
tools::checkRdaFiles(c("data/books.rda", "data/loans.rda", "R/sysdata.rda"))
#>                size ASCII compress version
#> data/books.rda  823 FALSE    bzip2       3
#> data/loans.rda 1040 FALSE    bzip2       3
#> R/sysdata.rda   105 FALSE    bzip2       3

# R/sysdata.rda holds objects for the package's own use.
internal <- new.env()
load("R/sysdata.rda", envir = internal)
ls(internal)
#> [1] "isbn_weights"
internal$isbn_weights
#>  [1] 1 3 1 3 1 3 1 3 1 3 1 3 1

# data/*.rda hold the exported datasets.
public <- new.env()
load("data/books.rda", envir = public)
load("data/loans.rda", envir = public)
sort(ls(public))
#> [1] "books" "loans"
shape <- \(d) paste(dim(d), collapse = " x ")
vapply(mget(c("books", "loans"), envir = public), shape, character(1L))
#>    books    loans
#> "16 x 6" "60 x 5"

Source: R documentation: checkRdaFiles and resaveRdaFiles

CRAN has a size rule that matters to anyone with a large dataset. The policy says that, as a general rule, neither data nor documentation should exceed 5MB (Publishing to CRAN has the details), that reasonable compression should be used, and that a large amount of data is better placed in a separate data-only package. Writing R Extensions adds that LazyDataCompression and the --data-compress option of R CMD INSTALL choose the compression of the installed lazy-load database, and that the only way to know which is best is to try them. R CMD build also has --resave-data, with no, gzip (the default) and best.

A dataset needs documentation as much as a function does, and an undocumented one is reported by R CMD check. The documentation of a dataset is a roxygen block above the name of the dataset as a string. The file below is R/data.R of shelf: it contains two blocks and no code that runs, because books and loans already exist in data/. The @format section and the \describe list are Rd, written by hand inside the roxygen block, and the Documentation with Rd, roxygen2 and Vignettes page explains each tag. The link [clean_books()] resolves to the help page of clean_books(), and the [books] link to the dataset’s own page; the two document() runs shown later explain why the first run complained about them.

#' The shelf catalogue
#'
#' Sixteen books of a small library, as they were typed into the catalogue:
#' titles with stray blanks and inconsistent case, two spellings of one
#' author, genres in several spellings, hyphenated and bare ISBNs (one
#' missing, one with a wrong check digit) and missing years and page counts.
#' [clean_books()] tidies it.
#'
#' @format A data frame with 16 rows and 6 columns:
#' \describe{
#'   \item{title}{Title (character).}
#'   \item{author}{Author (character).}
#'   \item{isbn}{ISBN-13, hyphenated or bare (character).}
#'   \item{year}{Publication year (integer).}
#'   \item{genre}{Genre (character).}
#'   \item{pages}{Number of pages (integer).}
#' }
#' @source Synthetic data generated for this package; the ISBNs have valid
#'   check digits but are not the ISBNs of real books.
#' @family datasets
"books"

#' The shelf loans
#'
#' Sixty loans of the books in [books] between January 2025 and June 2026.
#' One ISBN is a digit short, one member name is empty and others are spelt
#' inconsistently, one loan date was impossible and is `NA`, one return date
#' lies before its loan date and the last seven loans have not been returned.
#' [clean_loans()] tidies it.
#'
#' @format A data frame with 60 rows and 5 columns:
#' \describe{
#'   \item{loan_id}{`"L001"` to `"L060"` (character).}
#'   \item{isbn}{Bare ISBN-13 of the book (character).}
#'   \item{member}{Name of the member (character).}
#'   \item{loan_date}{Date the book was taken out (`Date`).}
#'   \item{return_date}{Date it was returned, `NA` while it is out (`Date`).}
#' }
#' @source Synthetic data generated for this package.
#' @family datasets
"loans"

Source: Writing R Extensions: Documenting data sets

The first line of each block is the title, the paragraph after it the description, and the last line, a bare string naming the object, is what roxygen2 documents. The roxygen2 8.0.0 NEWS says that documenting a value such as x <- 1:10 no longer adds the data-set markup, and that the way to document a dataset is the approach used here, a block above a string that names it.

Users reach the data in three ways, and the script that uses the installed package shows all three. The first is automatic: with LazyData, books is found as soon as library(shelf) has attached the package. The second is explicit and needs no attaching, shelf::books. The third is data(), which copies the dataset into the workspace; it is the only way when LazyData is false, and with LazyData: true it is rarely needed. The script also looks at the citation and at system.file(), which belong to the next section.

# Datasets declared with LazyData are visible once the package is attached.
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(shelf))
data(package = "shelf")$results[, c("Item", "Title")]
#>      Item    Title
#> [1,] "books" "The shelf catalogue"
#> [2,] "loans" "The shelf loans"
dim(books)
#> [1] 16  6
class(loans$loan_date)
#> [1] "Date"
exists("books")
#> [1] TRUE
environmentName(environment(clean_books))
#> [1] "shelf"

# Without attaching, ask for the dataset by name.
detach("package:shelf")
exists("books")
#> [1] FALSE
head(shelf::books$title, 3L)
#> [1] "The Dispossessed"     "Pride and Prejudice"  "  the quiet streets "
data("loans", package = "shelf")
exists("loans")
#> [1] TRUE
rm(loans)

# inst/CITATION is what citation() prints.
citation("shelf")
#> To cite package ‘shelf’ in publications use:
#>   Maintainers S (2026). _shelf: Tools for a Small Library Catalogue_. R
#>   package version 0.1.0.
#> A BibTeX entry for LaTeX users is
#>   @Manual{,
#>     title = {shelf: Tools for a Small Library Catalogue},
#>     author = {Shelf Maintainers},
#>     year = {2026},
#>     note = {R package version 0.1.0},
#>   }

# system.file() finds files under inst/ of the installed package.
file.exists(system.file("CITATION", package = "shelf"))
#> [1] TRUE
basename(system.file("doc", "shelf.html", package = "shelf"))
#> [1] "shelf.html"
nzchar(system.file("no", "such", "file", package = "shelf"))
#> [1] FALSE

Source: R documentation: data

A data image can contain references to the namespaces of packages that were used to create it, and Writing R Extensions warns that such references make it impossible to install the package if the other package is not a dependency. The check for this is manual: load all the images in a vanilla session, call str() on each, and look at loadedNamespaces(). A dataset of an S4 class that is defined in another package needs that package in Imports or Depends, and the manual suggests it may be wiser then to build the dataset from a data/foo.R script.

R/sysdata.rda

Some data are for the package and not for the user: a table of constants, a trained model, a lookup. shelf has one, the check-digit weights of an ISBN-13, which are 1 and 3 alternating. The weights could be a vector in a file of R/, and they are computed in data-raw/books.R so that the data-making is in one place. The file R/sysdata.rda is lazy-loaded into the namespace, so isbn_weights is visible to every function of the package and to nobody else (shelf:::isbn_weights reaches it, as the output in the previous section showed). usethis writes it with use_data(isbn_weights, internal = TRUE); note that this form saves every internal object into the one file, so all internal objects must be passed together, and that, unlike the files in data/, the objects of sysdata.rda follow the usual export rules, so a broad exportPattern() would export them. Writing R Extensions lists the file as one of two exceptions to the rule that R/ should contain code only; the other is files ending in .in, generated by a configure script. The R CMD check step "checking R/sysdata.rda" is the one that looks at it, and the installed package has sysdata.rdb and sysdata.rdx in R/, the lazy-load database.

inst/, system.file() and other installed files

Everything under inst/ is copied, unchanged, to the top level of the installed package. That makes inst/ the place for all files that are not R code, help or data in the R sense and still have to be present at run time, and it makes the names that R uses itself reserved: R, data, demo, exec, libs, man, help, html and Meta. The installed shelf shows the effect: inst/CITATION became CITATION, and the vignette that the build put in inst/doc is the doc directory.

Three things go in inst/ in nearly every package. inst/CITATION is the file that citation() reads, inst/extdata/ holds raw data files, and inst/doc/ is where the built vignettes go (you do not write it yourself: R CMD build does). Package-level information files such as AUTHORS or COPYRIGHTS and a NEWS.Rd for the news() function also go there. Files like README and ChangeLog at the top level of the source are ignored by R and are not installed, except for INDEX, LICENSE and NEWS (and, from R 4.6.0 on, README.md, which the NEWS says is now installed and shown in the HTML help), so a file that the user should see must be put in inst/.

Finding installed files with system.file()

A file in inst/extdata is not at a fixed path once the package is installed: the library can be anywhere. system.file() finds it, given the path inside the package and the package name, and returns the empty string when the file does not exist. That returns a different path in two of the five states of a package, and pkgload (the package behind devtools::load_all()) makes it work in both by replacing system.file() with a version that looks in inst/ of the source tree. The script shows both, on a copy of the package where data-raw/books.csv was copied to inst/extdata/books.csv: the package is first installed into a temporary library, and system.file() gives the path inside it, extdata/books.csv; then load_all() makes the same call return inst/extdata/books.csv.

# Raw files that the package needs at run time go under inst/. By
# convention inst/extdata holds data files; everything in inst/ lands in
# the top level of the installed package.
dir.create("inst/extdata", recursive = TRUE)
file.copy("data-raw/books.csv", "inst/extdata/books.csv")
#> [1] TRUE

# Installed: the file is at <package>/extdata/books.csv.
lib <- tempfile("lib")
dir.create(lib)
install.packages(".", repos = NULL, type = "source", lib = lib, quiet = TRUE)
installed <- system.file("extdata", "books.csv", package = "shelf",
                         lib.loc = lib)
sub(".*/shelf/", "", installed)
#> [1] "extdata/books.csv"
nrow(read.csv(installed))
#> [1] 16

# Under load_all() the same call is answered from the source tree, where
# the file is at inst/extdata/books.csv.
devtools::load_all(quiet = TRUE)
#> shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
dev <- system.file("extdata", "books.csv", package = "shelf")
sub(".*/shelf/", "", dev)
#> [1] "inst/extdata/books.csv"
identical(read.csv(dev), read.csv(installed))
#> [1] TRUE

# A path that does not exist gives the empty string, not an error.
system.file("extdata", "missing.csv", package = "shelf")
#> [1] ""
unlink(lib, recursive = TRUE)

Source: R documentation: system.file

The lesson is in the paths. Code that reads file.path("inst", "extdata", "books.csv") would work in the source tree and fail when installed; code that uses system.file("extdata", "books.csv", package = "shelf") works in both states, and returns "" (so the next read.csv() fails with a clear error) when the file is missing, which is also a reason to test the result with nzchar(). The same idea explains why paths in vignettes and examples are relative to the installed package and why tests use testthat::test_path() for fixtures, covered in Testing with testthat.

inst/CITATION

The CITATION file is parsed as R code and must contain calls to bibentry(); citation("shelf") prints it. If a package has no CITATION, R generates a citation from the DESCRIPTION, which is usually what you want, and Writing R Extensions recommends that a custom file start with citation(auto = meta) so that the entry for the package itself stays in step with the metadata, and then adds other works, such as a paper or a book. The file of shelf writes one entry by hand, which is simple and goes stale if the version changes.

bibentry(
  bibtype = "Manual",
  title = "shelf: Tools for a Small Library Catalogue",
  author = person("Shelf", "Maintainers"),
  year = "2026",
  note = "R package version 0.1.0"
)

Source: R documentation: citation and readCitationFile

The output of citation("shelf") in the previous section is this entry formatted twice, as text and as a BibTeX entry. The requirements are that the file produces no output when it is sourced and that it does not call functions that assume the package is installed, such as packageDescription(), because the file must work where the package is not installed in a library on the search path (the manual calls that essential for CRAN). An early draft of this file had a url field with a placeholder address, and R CMD check --as-cran reported it as not found, which is why it has none: the check looks up the URLs it finds in a package, so any link that goes into a package must exist.

The workflow with usethis and devtools

Making a package by hand means creating dozens of small files with the right names and the right contents, and then running a handful of R CMD commands in the right order. Two community packages automate it, and between them they have become the usual way to write a package. usethis (the use_* functions) creates and edits the files of a package and a project: it writes DESCRIPTION, adds a licence, a test directory, a vignette, a dependency. devtools (and the packages behind it: pkgload, pkgbuild, rcmdcheck, roxygen2 and testthat) runs the development loop: load the code, document it, test it, check it, install it. They are not part of R, and everything they do can be done with R CMD and an editor, as the next section shows; what they save is time and typing mistakes.

Task With usethis and devtools Without them

Create the package

usethis::create_package("~/shelf")

Create the directory and write DESCRIPTION and NAMESPACE by hand, or package.skeleton().

Add a source file

usethis::use_r("isbn")

Create R/isbn.R in an editor.

Declare a dependency

usethis::use_package("withr", "Suggests")

Edit the field of DESCRIPTION.

Add a licence

usethis::use_mit_license()

Write the License field and the LICENSE file.

Try the code

devtools::load_all()

R CMD INSTALL shelf then library(shelf) in a new session.

Write help and NAMESPACE

devtools::document()

Write the Rd files and the NAMESPACE by hand.

Run the tests

devtools::test()

The tests run inside R CMD check; or Rscript tests/testthat.R against an installed package.

Check the package

devtools::check()

R CMD build shelf and then R CMD check --as-cran shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz.

Install it

devtools::install()

R CMD INSTALL shelf or R CMD INSTALL shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz.

Build the bundle

devtools::build()

R CMD build shelf.

Add data

usethis::use_data_raw() and usethis::use_data()

Write the script, call save() into data/.

Add a vignette

usethis::use_vignette("shelf")

Create vignettes/shelf.Rmd and edit DESCRIPTION.

Add tests

usethis::use_testthat(3) and usethis::use_test("isbn")

Create tests/testthat.R and the test files.

Source: usethis package documentation: Reference

The loop that a package author runs many times a day is shorter than the table suggests. Edit a file in R/; press the shortcut for load_all(), which loads the package from its source in a second and attaches it as if it were installed; try the function in the console, or run the tests with devtools::test(); add or change a roxygen block, and run document(); and now and then run check(). Only the last of those is slow, and the other four are what makes writing a package pleasant. load_all() does not run R CMD INSTALL: it reads the files of R/, evaluates them into a namespace, loads the data, runs the load hooks and attaches the package, but it does not lazy-load or byte-compile anything, and it replaces system.file() (as shown earlier) so that files of inst/ are found. The differences are what the other states of the package are for, and check() is how they are tested.

A few more of the use_* functions belong to the life of a package and are only named here, because they change a Git repository or talk to GitHub and are not run on this page. They are fragments, shown so that their names are known.

# Fragment, not run: they create a Git repository and talk to GitHub.
usethis::use_git()
usethis::use_github()
usethis::use_readme_rmd()
usethis::use_github_action("check-standard")

Source: usethis package documentation: use_git

use_git() initialises a repository and offers a first commit, use_github() creates the repository on GitHub and pushes, use_readme_rmd() writes a README.Rmd (and a git hook that keeps it in step with the README.md), and use_github_action() adds a workflow that runs R CMD check on every push. The releases are a chain of use_news_md(), use_cran_comments(), use_version() and devtools::release(), and they belong to Publishing to CRAN.

What devtools::check() adds to R CMD check

devtools::check() is R CMD build followed by R CMD check, but with a set of choices made for you. It documents the package first, if the installed roxygen2 matches the version recorded in DESCRIPTION; it builds the bundle in a temporary directory and checks that; it sets the compiler flags -Wall -pedantic; it runs the check with --as-cran (its cran = TRUE default, which the documentation says is a best-effort copy of what CRAN does and more than the flag alone); it sets NOT_CRAN=true, which testthat reads to decide whether to run tests marked skip_on_cran(); and it switches off the checks that need the network or a complete set of suggested packages: the remote part of the CRAN incoming check and the incoming check itself, the requirement that all suggested packages be installed (_R_CHECK_FORCE_SUGGESTS_) and the report of unused imports (_R_CHECK_PACKAGES_USED_IGNORE_UNUSED_IMPORTS_). The log of the real run on shelf prints exactly these settings, and the report at the end is formatted by rcmdcheck: errors, warnings and notes counted, and each one explained. Its output is shown in full in the step-by-step section below.

build(), install() and what devtools offers now

The two remaining functions of the table turn the source into the second and the fourth state. devtools::build() runs R CMD build through pkgbuild and, unless it is told otherwise, puts the tarball in the parent directory of the package, which is also where the command line puts it. The script builds the package, checks where the file went and removes the file again.

# build() runs R CMD build. By default the tarball goes to the parent of the
# package directory, which is where R CMD build leaves it too.
path <- devtools::build(quiet = FALSE)
#> ── R CMD build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> * checking for file ‘~/shelf/DESCRIPTION’ ... OK
#> * preparing ‘shelf’:
#> * checking DESCRIPTION meta-information ... OK
#> * installing the package (it is needed to build vignettes)
#> * creating vignettes ... OK
#> * checking for LF line-endings in source and make files and shell scripts
#> * checking for empty or unneeded directories
#> * building ‘shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz’
basename(path)
#> [1] "shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz"
identical(dirname(path), dirname(getwd()))
#> [1] TRUE
file.exists(path)
#> [1] TRUE

# Only the tarball is kept for the next steps, so remove this one.
unlink(path)
file.exists(path)
#> [1] FALSE

Source: devtools package documentation: build

devtools::install() installs the package. Its documentation says that it uses R CMD INSTALL after installing the needed dependencies with pak::local_install_deps(), and by default it builds the package first, so that the installation comes from a clean tarball. To install somewhere else than the first library, the documentation suggests withr::with_libpaths(), which the script does with a temporary library, so that no other library changes. Three kinds of lines are left out of the output because they show paths of the machine that ran it: the library paths that pak lists, the path of the temporary tarball and the installation directory.

# install() builds the package and installs it with R CMD INSTALL. Here it
# goes to a temporary library so that no other library changes.
lib <- tempfile("library")
dir.create(lib)
withr::with_libpaths(lib, devtools::install(quiet = FALSE), action = "prefix")
#> ── pak::local_install_deps() ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>
#>
#> ℹ No downloads are needed
#> ── R CMD build ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> * checking for file ‘~/shelf/DESCRIPTION’ ... OK
#> * preparing ‘shelf’:
#> * checking DESCRIPTION meta-information ... OK
#> * checking for LF line-endings in source and make files and shell scripts
#> * checking for empty or unneeded directories
#> * building ‘shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz’
#> ── R CMD INSTALL ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> * installing *source* package ‘shelf’ ...
#> ** this is package ‘shelf’ version ‘0.1.0’
#> ** using staged installation
#> ** R
#> ** data
#> *** moving datasets to lazyload DB
#> ** inst
#> ** tests
#> ** byte-compile and prepare package for lazy loading
#> ** help
#> *** installing help indices
#> ** building package indices
#> ** installing vignettes
#> ** testing if installed package can be loaded from temporary location
#> ** testing if installed package can be loaded from final location
#> ** testing if installed package keeps a record of temporary installation path
#> * DONE (shelf)
list.files(lib)
#> [1] "shelf"
packageVersion("shelf", lib.loc = lib)
#> [1] ‘0.1.0’

Source: devtools package documentation: install

The --install-tests option that devtools passes (the line that was left out) installs the tests/ directory into the library, so that the tests can be run against the installed package afterwards. The messages after the R CMD INSTALL heading are the ones that the R CMD INSTALL section below explains line by line.

devtools has also shrunk over the years, and a tutorial that is a few years old may name functions that no longer exist in it. The last script lists which of the functions of this page devtools 2.5.2 exports and which it does not, and prints the body of the deprecated create().

# What devtools 2.5.2 still offers, and what it hands over to other packages.
exports <- getNamespaceExports("devtools")
c(
  load_all = "load_all" %in% exports,
  document = "document" %in% exports,
  test = "test" %in% exports,
  check = "check" %in% exports,
  build = "build" %in% exports,
  install = "install" %in% exports,
  use_testthat = "use_testthat" %in% exports,
  create_package = "create_package" %in% exports
)
#>       load_all       document           test          check          build
#>           TRUE           TRUE           TRUE           TRUE           TRUE
#>        install   use_testthat create_package
#>           TRUE          FALSE          FALSE

# create() is only a deprecated wrapper around usethis::create_package().
deparse(body(devtools::create))
#> [1] "{"
#> [2] "    lifecycle::deprecate_warn(\"2.5.0\", \"create()\", \"usethis::create_package()\")"
#> [3] "    usethis::create_package(path, ..., open = open)"
#> [4] "}"

Source: devtools package documentation: Reference

The loop functions (load_all(), document(), test(), check(), build() and install()) are devtools’s; use_testthat() and create_package() are not exported by it any more because they belong to usethis, and create() is a deprecated wrapper that calls usethis::create_package() and warns, with the version of devtools in which the deprecation started (2.5.0) as an argument of the warning.

The shelf package, step by step

This section builds shelf the way a person would, one step at a time. The output of each step is the real output of the call as the tools printed it, taken from the recorded session in which the package was made, with ~/shelf for the package directory. The calls are fragments of that session, in the order in which they were made, and each assumes the effect of the earlier ones (the active project, the working directory). The calls say usethis:: in front of every function, which is how they were recorded; in an interactive session one would run library(usethis) or library(devtools) once and drop the prefixes.

Step 1: create the package

create_package() creates the directory, the R/ subdirectory, DESCRIPTION and NAMESPACE. The call gives the title, version, description and authors, so that the file is right at once; in an interactive session create_package("~/shelf") alone is enough and the fields are edited in DESCRIPTION afterwards. rstudio = FALSE skips the RStudio project file and open = FALSE keeps the session where it is. proj_set() tells usethis which project the next calls apply to, because create_package() did not switch the session to the new project. The DESCRIPTION that usethis prints is the file it just wrote, with Authors@R shown parsed; License is still a hint, and Config/roxygen2/version and Roxygen were added by usethis because roxygen2 is the default way to document.

usethis::create_package(
  "~/shelf",
  fields = list(
    Title = "Tools for a Small Library Catalogue",
    Version = "0.1.0",
    Description = paste(
      "Cleans a small library catalogue and its loans table, validates",
      "ISBN-13 strings, and reports overdue loans and overdue rates by",
      "genre. Ships the example 'books' and 'loans' datasets used by the",
      "documentation."
    ),
    `Authors@R` = paste0(
      'person("Shelf", "Maintainers", email = "maintainer@example.com", ',
      'role = c("aut", "cre", "cph"))'
    )
  ),
  rstudio = FALSE, open = FALSE
)
usethis::proj_set("~/shelf")
#> ✔ Creating '~/shelf/'.
#> ✔ Setting active project to "~/shelf".
#> ✔ Creating 'R/'.
#> ✔ Writing 'DESCRIPTION'.
#> Package: shelf
#> Title: Tools for a Small Library Catalogue
#> Version: 0.1.0
#> Authors@R (parsed):
#>     * Shelf Maintainers <maintainer@example.com> [aut, cre, cph]
#> Description: Cleans a small library catalogue and its loans table,
#>     validates ISBN-13 strings, and reports overdue loans and overdue rates
#>     by genre. Ships the example 'books' and 'loans' datasets used by the
#>     documentation.
#> License: `use_mit_license()`, `use_gpl3_license()` or friends to pick a
#>     license
#> Config/roxygen2/version: 8.1.1
#> Encoding: UTF-8
#> Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE)
#> ✔ Writing 'NAMESPACE'.
#> ✔ Setting active project to "<no active project>".
#> ✔ Setting active project to "~/shelf".

Source: usethis package documentation: create_package

The recorded script wrote the Authors@R string on one line; it is split over two here for width.

Step 2: the licence

use_mit_license() wrote the field, the two-line LICENSE file and the full LICENSE.md, and added the .Rbuildignore entry that keeps the long file out of the bundle. The Authors@R person has the role cph, but the function was called without a name and used the default copyright holder, which is why the LICENSE file said shelf authors earlier.

usethis::use_mit_license()
#> ✔ Adding "MIT + file LICENSE" to 'License'.
#> ✔ Writing 'LICENSE'.
#> ✔ Writing 'LICENSE.md'.
#> ✔ Adding "^LICENSE\\.md$" to '.Rbuildignore'.

Source: usethis package documentation: licenses

Step 3: tests

use_testthat(3) made tests/testthat/, the runner tests/testthat.R, added testthat to Suggests with a minimum version, and set the testthat edition in Config/testthat/edition. It suggests the next call, use_test(), which creates a test file. The tests themselves are the subject of Testing with testthat.

usethis::use_testthat(3)
#> ✔ Adding testthat to 'Suggests' field in DESCRIPTION.
#> ✔ Adding "3" to 'Config/testthat/edition'.
#> ✔ Creating 'tests/testthat/'.
#> ✔ Writing 'tests/testthat.R'.
#> ☐ Call `usethis::use_test()` to initialize a basic test file and open it for
#>   editing.

Source: usethis package documentation: use_testthat

Step 4: dependencies

Two dependencies are declared: R itself, in Depends, and withr, in Suggests. The first call is the one that adds Depends: R (>= 4.1.0), and it is made for the reason that the earlier section on dependencies gave: R/isbn.R uses the \(i) shorthand. The second adds the package that the tests use to set options temporarily, and prints the advice for a suggested package.

usethis::use_package("R", "Depends", "4.1.0")
#> ✔ Adding R to 'Depends' field in DESCRIPTION.
usethis::use_package("withr", "Suggests")
#> ✔ Adding withr to 'Suggests' field in DESCRIPTION.
#> ☐ Use `requireNamespace("withr", quietly = TRUE)` to test if withr is
#>   installed.
#> ☐ Then directly refer to functions with `withr::fun()`.

Source: usethis package documentation: use_package

Step 5: a vignette

use_vignette() creates vignettes/shelf.Rmd from a template, adds knitr and rmarkdown to Suggests, names knitr in VignetteBuilder, and keeps the built output of the vignette out of Git (inst/doc in .gitignore, and *.html and *.R in vignettes/.gitignore). The template was then replaced by the real vignette, which the documentation page explains.

usethis::use_vignette("shelf", "Analysing library loans with shelf")
#> ✔ Adding knitr to 'Suggests' field in DESCRIPTION.
#> ✔ Adding "inst/doc" to '.gitignore'.
#> ✔ Adding rmarkdown to 'Suggests' field in DESCRIPTION.
#> ✔ Adding "knitr" to 'VignetteBuilder'.
#> ✔ Creating 'vignettes/'.
#> ✔ Adding "*.html" and "*.R" to 'vignettes/.gitignore'.
#> ✔ Writing 'vignettes/shelf.Rmd'.
#> ☐ Edit 'vignettes/shelf.Rmd'.

Source: usethis package documentation: use_vignette

Step 6: raw data, news, comments for CRAN, citation, lintr

A group of calls creates the other files that a package has. use_data_raw() makes data-raw/books.R and puts ^data-raw$ into .Rbuildignore. use_news_md() writes NEWS.md, use_cran_comments() writes cran-comments.md (a file for the submission, excluded from the bundle) and use_citation() writes a template inst/CITATION. lintr::use_lintr() is not a usethis function: it writes the .lintr configuration and, in a package, adds it to .Rbuildignore itself. usethis’s use_build_ignore() is the general way to exclude a file from the bundle; called after use_lintr(), it finds the entry already there and prints nothing.

usethis::use_data_raw("books", open = FALSE)
#> ✔ Creating 'data-raw/'.
#> ✔ Adding "^data-raw$" to '.Rbuildignore'.
#> ✔ Writing 'data-raw/books.R'.
#> ☐ Finish writing the data preparation script in 'data-raw/books.R'.
#> ☐ Use `usethis::use_data()` to add prepared data to package.
usethis::use_news_md(open = FALSE)
#> ✔ Writing 'NEWS.md'.
usethis::use_cran_comments(open = FALSE)
#> ✔ Writing 'cran-comments.md'.
#> ✔ Adding "^cran-comments\\.md$" to '.Rbuildignore'.
usethis::use_citation()
#> ✔ Creating 'inst/'.
#> ✔ Writing 'inst/CITATION'.
#> ☐ Edit 'inst/CITATION'.
lintr::use_lintr(path = usethis::proj_get(), type = "tidyverse")
#> Added ^\.lintr$ to `.Rbuildignore`.
usethis::use_build_ignore(".lintr")

The templates were then replaced by the real data-raw/books.R, inst/CITATION, NEWS.md, cran-comments.md and the files of R/, tests/testthat/ and vignettes/, which were copied into place. Everything that follows is that code.

Step 7: the R code

The code of shelf is five files and the hooks. The excerpts below show what is specific to a package; each file of the finished tree continues in the same style. R/isbn.R holds ISBN handling: normalise_isbn() drops everything except digits and X, is_valid_isbn13() checks the length and the check digit, and squish() is a private helper. Two details of it are about packages. The function uses the \(i) shorthand for the anonymous function passed to vapply(), which is why the package declares R 4.1.0. And it uses isbn_weights, the object from R/sysdata.rda, which does not exist in any file of R/ and is created in step 8. The documentation comments above the functions are roxygen2: @export tags make the NAMESPACE, @param and @returns the help page, and @examples the examples that R CMD check runs.

#' Normalise and validate ISBN-13 strings
#'
#' `normalise_isbn()` drops everything except digits and `X` and upper-cases
#' the result, so `"978-0-00-100010-0"` and `"9780001000100"` compare equal.
#' `is_valid_isbn13()` checks that a (normalised) string has 13 digits and a
#' correct check digit: the digits are multiplied alternately by 1 and 3 and
#' the sum must be divisible by 10.
#'
#' @param x A character vector of ISBNs; `NA` and empty strings are allowed.
#' @returns `normalise_isbn()` returns a character vector of the same length;
#'   `is_valid_isbn13()` a logical vector of the same length, `FALSE` for
#'   `NA` and for the empty string.
#' @examples
#' normalise_isbn("978-0-00-100010-0")
#' is_valid_isbn13(c("978-0-00-100010-0", "9780001000101", "", NA))
#' @export
normalise_isbn <- function(x) {
  gsub("[^0-9X]", "", toupper(x))
}

#' @rdname normalise_isbn
#' @export
is_valid_isbn13 <- function(x) {
  digits <- normalise_isbn(x)
  ok <- !is.na(digits) & nchar(digits) == 13L &
    !grepl("X", digits, fixed = TRUE)
  vapply(seq_along(digits), \(i) {
    if (!ok[[i]]) {
      return(FALSE)
    }
    d <- as.integer(strsplit(digits[[i]], "")[[1L]])
    sum(d * isbn_weights) %% 10L == 0L
  }, logical(1L))
}

# Collapse runs of blanks and trim the ends; NA stays NA.
squish <- function(x) {
  gsub(" +", " ", trimws(x))
}

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: Getting started

R/book.R is the book class of the scenario in the three-function form that Advanced R (a community book) recommends and the S3 page of this reference explains: a low-level constructor new_book() that only checks types, a validator validate_book() that checks values, and a friendly helper book() that cleans its input and calls both. The print, format and summary methods are registered with @export, which roxygen2 turns into the S3method() lines seen above. The block named book-methods documents the four methods in one help page by putting @rdname on each of them, after an empty NULL object that carries the page. The excerpt shows the documented book() constructor and that block with the first method, format.book(); the validator, the other three methods and the rest of the file are left out. The class design itself is in S3 Classes and Generics.

#' The `book` class
#'
#' `book()` is the user-facing constructor of the `book` class: it trims the
#' text fields, normalises the ISBN with [normalise_isbn()], coerces `year`
#' and `pages` to integer and validates the result. `new_book()` is the
#' low-level constructor that only checks types, and `validate_book()` checks
#' the values; both are exported so that other packages can extend the class.
#'
#' @param title Title of the book (a single string).
#' @param author Author (a single string, or `NA`).
#' @param isbn ISBN-13, hyphenated or bare (a single string, or `NA`).
#' @param year Publication year (a single number, or `NA`).
#' @param genre Genre (a single string, or `NA`).
#' @param pages Number of pages (a single number, or `NA`).
#' @returns An object of class `book`: a list with the six fields above, each
#'   of length one.
#' @examples
#' b <- book("  the quiet streets ", "Mara Quill", "978-0-00-100010-0", 2019,
#'           "Fiction ", 214)
#' b
#' summary(b)
#' unclass(b)
#' @family book class
#' @export
book <- function(title, author = NA_character_, isbn = NA_character_,
                 year = NA_integer_, genre = NA_character_,
                 pages = NA_integer_) {
  validate_book(new_book(
    title = squish(title),
    author = squish(author),
    isbn = if (is.na(isbn)) NA_character_ else normalise_isbn(isbn),
    year = as.integer(year),
    genre = squish(genre),
    pages = as.integer(pages)
  ))
}
# [...]
#' Methods for the `book` class
#'
#' `format()` renders a book as `"<title> (<author>, <year>)"`, `print()`
#' shows that line with a `<book>` marker and `summary()` returns a small
#' `summary.book` object with its own print method.
#'
#' @param x,object A `book` object (for `print.summary.book()`, a
#'   `summary.book` object).
#' @param ... Ignored, present for compatibility with the generics.
#' @returns `format.book()` returns a string; `print.book()` and
#'   `print.summary.book()` return their argument invisibly;
#'   `summary.book()` returns a list of class `summary.book` with the
#'   elements `title`, `has_isbn` and `pages`.
#' @examples
#' b <- book("Salt and Static", "Mara Quill", "978-0-01-400145-3", 2018,
#'           "Mystery", 244)
#' format(b)
#' print(b)
#' s <- summary(b)
#' class(s)
#' s
#' @family book class
#' @name book-methods
NULL

#' @rdname book-methods
#' @export
format.book <- function(x, ...) {
  year <- if (is.na(x$year)) "n.d." else x$year
  sprintf("%s (%s, %s)", x$title, x$author, year)
}

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: Documenting S3

R/clean.R has the two cleaning functions, clean_books() and clean_loans(), which turn the messy books and loans of the scenario into tidy ones. R/loans.R has the analyses: overdue_loans() (which takes today and loan_days as arguments with defaults that come from shelf_today() and from the shelf.loan_days option that .onLoad() sets), loan_summary() and loans_per_month(). The small function shelf_today() wraps the call that returns the current date, so that tests can replace it, as explained in the section on the R/ directory. The excerpts stop after clean_books() and after shelf_today(); clean_loans(), loan_summary() and loans_per_month() follow in the same style.

#' Clean the catalogue and the loans table
#'
#' `clean_books()` trims and squishes `title` and `author`, lower-cases and
#' trims `genre`, and replaces `isbn` by its normalised form, with `NA` where
#' the ISBN is empty or fails the check digit. `clean_loans()` parses the two
#' date columns when they are still text, trims `member` (an empty member
#' becomes `NA`) and sets a `return_date` that lies before the `loan_date` to
#' `NA`, because such a return cannot have happened.
#'
#' @param books A data frame with the columns of [books].
#' @param loans A data frame with the columns of [loans]; `loan_date` and
#'   `return_date` may be `Date` or ISO 8601 strings.
#' @returns A data frame with the same columns and rows as the input.
#' @examples
#' head(clean_books(books), 4)
#' sum(is.na(clean_books(books)$isbn))
#' str(clean_loans(loans))
#' @family cleaning
#' @export
clean_books <- function(books) {
  books$title <- squish(books$title)
  books$author <- squish(books$author)
  books$genre <- tolower(squish(books$genre))
  isbn <- normalise_isbn(books$isbn)
  isbn[!is_valid_isbn13(isbn)] <- NA_character_
  books$isbn <- isbn
  books
}

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: Documenting functions

#' Overdue loans
#'
#' A loan is overdue when it was returned more than `loan_days` days after it
#' was taken out, or when it has not been returned and `today` is more than
#' `loan_days` days after the loan date. Loans whose `loan_date` is `NA` are
#' never reported.
#'
#' @param loans A data frame with the columns of [loans], with `loan_date`
#'   and `return_date` as `Date` (see [clean_loans()]).
#' @param today The reference date for loans that are still out. Defaults to
#'   the current date.
#' @param loan_days Length of the loan period in days. Defaults to the
#'   `shelf.loan_days` option, which the package sets to 21 when it is loaded.
#' @returns The overdue rows of `loans` with an extra integer column
#'   `days_out`: the days from the loan date to the return date, or to
#'   `today` for a loan that is still out.
#' @examples
#' out <- overdue_loans(loans, today = as.Date("2026-06-30"))
#' nrow(out)
#' head(out[order(-out$days_out), ], 3)
#' @family loan analyses
#' @export
overdue_loans <- function(loans, today = shelf_today(),
                          loan_days = getOption("shelf.loan_days", 21L)) {
  end <- loans$return_date
  end[is.na(end)] <- today
  days_out <- as.integer(end - loans$loan_date)
  keep <- !is.na(days_out) & days_out > loan_days
  loans <- loans[keep, , drop = FALSE]
  loans$days_out <- days_out[keep]
  rownames(loans) <- NULL
  loans
}

# The reference date; kept as a function so that tests can replace it.
shelf_today <- function() {
  Sys.Date()
}

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: Reusing documentation

The remaining two files, R/data.R (the documentation of the two datasets) and R/zzz.R (the hooks), were shown earlier. The package sources pass lintr’s lint_package(); the script below runs it on the finished tree. The test helper calls testthat::test_path(), so the script attaches testthat first, as the test runner does.

# lintr sees the whole package, so it knows which names are defined in
# the other files of R/ and in R/sysdata.rda. The test helper calls
# testthat::test_path(), so testthat is attached first, as it is when the
# tests run.
library(testthat)
lintr::lint_package()
#> ℹ No lints found.

Source: lintr package documentation: lint_package

Linting one file at a time is less helpful for a package. lintr’s object_usage_linter looks for names that are used and not defined, and a single file of shelf uses names defined in its neighbours (squish() in book.R, or isbn_weights in isbn.R), so it reports them as "no visible global function definition". lint_package() knows the whole package and reports nothing; it is also what the .lintr file configures. Style, Linting and Static Analysis covers the linters.

Step 8: the data

The recipe for the data is the script data-raw/books.R. It reads the two CSV files that sit next to it (the same books.csv and loans.csv as the scenario), parses the dates of the loans, saves the two data frames with use_data(), and then makes the internal object, a vector of the thirteen check-digit weights, with use_data(internal = TRUE). It is a package source and is run from the package root, as source("data-raw/books.R").

# Build the `books` and `loans` datasets from the CSV files in data-raw/.
books <- read.csv("data-raw/books.csv")
loans <- read.csv("data-raw/loans.csv", colClasses = "character")
loans$loan_date <- as.Date(loans$loan_date, format = "%Y-%m-%d")
loans$return_date <- as.Date(loans$return_date, format = "%Y-%m-%d")
usethis::use_data(books, loans, overwrite = TRUE)

# Internal data: the ISBN-13 check-digit weights used by is_valid_isbn13().
isbn_weights <- rep(c(1L, 3L), length.out = 13L)
usethis::use_data(isbn_weights, internal = TRUE, overwrite = TRUE)

Step 9: document

devtools::document() runs roxygen2: it reads the comments above the functions and writes the Rd files of man/ and the NAMESPACE. It was run twice, and the two runs print different things. The first run found no man/ directory, so every link in the comments to a topic of the package itself, written in Markdown as [normalise_isbn()] or [books], pointed at a help page that did not exist yet and was reported as one that "could not be resolved"; the run wrote all of the files in spite of that, the message says that it is "normal" until the topic is documented, and the second run, which could see the pages written by the first, is silent. Two of the ten warnings are shown, the first and the last, and the others are of the same kind. A package author who sees this message once on a new package has nothing to fix.

Source: devtools package documentation: document

The line marked [...] stands for the other eight warnings of the first run. The recorded creation session printed the same messages, with the same ten links, and both runs wrote the same NAMESPACE and the same nine Rd files. One of the files that it wrote is man/normalise_isbn.Rd. It shows what roxygen2 does with a block: the first paragraph of the comment became \title, the second \description, @param became \arguments, @returns became \value, @examples became \examples, and two functions documented in one block share the \name and have an \alias each, with their calls listed together in \usage. The first two lines say that the file is generated and which source file to edit.

\alias{normalise_isbn}
\alias{is_valid_isbn13}
\title{Normalise and validate ISBN-13 strings}
\usage{
normalise_isbn(x)

is_valid_isbn13(x)
}
\arguments{
\item{x}{A character vector of ISBNs; \code{NA} and empty strings are allowed.}
}
\value{
\code{normalise_isbn()} returns a character vector of the same length;
\code{is_valid_isbn13()} a logical vector of the same length, \code{FALSE} for
\code{NA} and for the empty string.
}
\description{
\code{normalise_isbn()} drops everything except digits and \code{X} and upper-cases
the result, so \code{"978-0-00-100010-0"} and \code{"9780001000100"} compare equal.
\code{is_valid_isbn13()} checks that a (normalised) string has 13 digits and a
correct check digit: the digits are multiplied alternately by 1 and 3 and
the sum must be divisible by 10.
}
\examples{

is_valid_isbn13(c("978-0-00-100010-0", "9780001000101", "", NA))

Source: Writing R Extensions: Rd format

The first line of that file ("do not edit by hand") is the rule of the workflow: the comments in R/ are the source and man/ is generated, so the generated files are committed to the repository (CRAN needs them in the bundle) but never edited. shelf has nine of them, and the NAMESPACE shown in the section above is the other generated file. The run on the copy that the page uses agrees: the Rd files and the NAMESPACE that document() wrote there are the same as those in the finished package.

devtools::load_all() attaches the package from its source. A package can also be tested without devtools: R CMD check runs everything in tests/, and testthat.R is the file that does it (library(testthat), library(shelf) and test_check("shelf")). In an R CMD check run (the section on R CMD check below shows one) the tests run against the installed package, and two of them are skipped because NOT_CRAN is not set there, as the summary line in the check log shows: the test in test-loans.R that calls skip_on_cran(), and the snapshot test in test-book.R, whose expect_snapshot() is not verified on CRAN; devtools::check() sets NOT_CRAN, so under it nothing is skipped. The test coverage of the package, measured once with covr 3.6.5, was 93.81 %: R/zzz.R was at 40 % because .onAttach() runs only when the package is attached (and the tests do not attach it), R/loans.R at 96.43 % and the other three files at 100 %. The details of the testing tools are the subject of Testing with testthat.

devtools::check() is the step that finds what the earlier ones did not. The call below skips the PDF manual (manual = FALSE), because making it needs a TeX installation, which the machine where this page was checked does not have. The long list of checks in between is shown, in its longer R CMD check --as-cran form, in the next section. The summary also prints the time that the check took, which is left out.

That is the package. Everything from here on is how it travels: R CMD build makes a bundle of it, R CMD check checks the bundle, R CMD INSTALL installs it, and library() loads it, the same four states of the figure, done with the commands that ship with R.

R CMD build, INSTALL and check without devtools

Everything the devtools functions do for the last three steps is done by three commands that ship with R and run in a shell, not in an R session: R CMD build, R CMD check and R CMD INSTALL. They are the commands that CRAN and every continuous-integration service run, their messages are the ones that the earlier sections quoted, and a person who has met them once can read any build or check log. The commands below were run from the directory that contains the package directory shelf, because that is where R CMD build shelf leaves its tarball and where R CMD check leaves the shelf.Rcheck directory; the commands are shown as they were typed, and the paths in the output were shortened.

The three commands take a package from one state to the next. R CMD build turns the source directory (state 1) into the tarball (state 2). R CMD check takes the tarball, installs it into a scratch library, and runs every kind of test on the result. R CMD INSTALL turns the directory or the tarball into an installed package (state 4), and with --build it also leaves a binary package (state 3). The sections follow that order.

R CMD build

R CMD build makes the bundle. It reads .Rbuildignore and leaves out what it lists, builds the vignettes (which needs the package itself installed in a temporary library), makes a few clean-ups, and writes <package>_<version>.tar.gz, taking both names from DESCRIPTION.

R CMD build shelf

Source: R documentation: R CMD build and R CMD check

The log that it printed is the same one that devtools::build() showed earlier, apart from the first heading.

* building ‘shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz’

Source: Writing R Extensions: Building package tarballs

Each line is a step. checking for file ‘shelf/DESCRIPTION’ and checking DESCRIPTION meta-information read the metadata and refuse a package that has no valid one. installing the package (it is needed to build vignettes) and creating vignettes are present because the package has a vignettes/ directory and a VignetteBuilder field; a package with no vignettes and no dynamic Rd content skips both lines (the manual says that the temporary installation is also what runs the \Sexpr macros of the Rd files, and R NEWS: Changes in R 4.2.0 records that a package whose only dynamic content is the \doi macro is built without it). checking for LF line-endings converts the line endings of the source and Makefile files of src/ when needed, and checking for empty or unneeded directories removes directories that have nothing in them, because an empty directory in a tarball is usually a mistake. The last line names the tarball.

The options of the command are the ones that the tool prints for itself, and the next block is that help text. The ones that matter in practice are --no-build-vignettes (the run of the earlier experiment), --resave-data, which recompresses the .rda files of data/ as the checks of the data section suggest, --compression and --no-manual. --md5 and --sha256 add checksum files to the tarball, and --sha256 is new in R 4.6.0 (R NEWS: Changes in R 4.6.0: the file is generated by default by R CMD INSTALL --build and optionally by R CMD build --sha256). --user (R 4.4.0) overrides the user name that R CMD build records in the Packaged field, which is the line that tells a reader who built the tarball and when.

R CMD build --help

Source: R documentation: R CMD build and R CMD check

  --no-resave-data      same as --resave-data=no

Source: Writing R Extensions: Building package tarballs

Compare the list with the tree of the source package. Four things are gone: .lintr, cran-comments.md, LICENSE.md and the whole of data-raw/ are the entries that .Rbuildignore lists, and the file .Rbuildignore itself is not in the bundle either. Three things were added: inst/doc/ holds the built vignette in three forms (shelf.html, the tangled code shelf.R and the source shelf.Rmd), build/vignette.rds is an index of the built vignettes (the installed package has a Meta/vignette.rds of its own, as the binary listing below shows), and the directory entries are explicit. The tests/testthat/_snaps/book.md snapshot, the fixture and the helper are in because tests belong to the package.

Two warnings about the build step are worth knowing. The first is about vignettes: a package whose bundle was built with --no-build-vignettes has a vignettes/ directory and no inst/doc, and the check reports it (see the next section for the real output). The second is that the build can change DESCRIPTION: the missing Depends: R (>= ...) warnings of the dependency section are printed by the build step and written into the bundle’s DESCRIPTION, so a bundle is not always byte-for-byte the source that went in.

R CMD check

R CMD check is the step that finds what the earlier ones did not. Given a bundle, it unpacks it into <package>.Rcheck/00_pkg_src, installs it into <package>.Rcheck, and runs a long list of checks on the files, the code, the documentation, the data, the examples, the tests and the vignettes. The form used for a CRAN submission and for every output on this page is the one with --as-cran. --no-manual is added because the PDF manual needs a TeX installation, and _R_CHECK_CRAN_INCOMING_REMOTE_=false is set so that the check does not try to reach CRAN: the part on the incoming checks, below, shows what happens when it does.

_R_CHECK_CRAN_INCOMING_REMOTE_=false R CMD check --as-cran --no-manual shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz

Reading that list from the top is a tour of everything that a package promises. The table groups the checks by what they look at, and it is the best map of what a package author is responsible for.

Checks (the words of the log) What they look at Where the answer is fixed

checking for file ‘shelf/DESCRIPTION’, package encoding, DESCRIPTION meta-information, CRAN incoming feasibility

The metadata: required fields, a valid version and licence, a maintainer, a name that does not clash on CRAN.

DESCRIPTION

checking package namespace information, if there is a namespace, package dependencies, dependencies in R code, use of S3 registration, S3 generic/method consistency, replacement functions

That the NAMESPACE is valid, that every package used is declared, that each S3 method is registered and agrees with its generic.

NAMESPACE, Imports, Suggests

checking for executable files, hidden files and directories, portable file names, sufficient/correct file permissions, top-level files, left-over files, package subdirectories, ‘build’ directory, future file timestamps

The tree of the bundle: no binaries, no hidden files, portable names, no file that R does not know at the top level, no file dated in the future.

.Rbuildignore, the directory itself

checking whether package ‘shelf’ can be installed, installed package size, loading without being on the library search path, whether the package can be loaded, whether the package can be unloaded cleanly, whether startup messages can be suppressed

The installation, the size of the installed package, loading, unloading, and that every start-up message is a packageStartupMessage().

R/, R/zzz.R

checking code files for non-ASCII characters, R files for syntax errors, foreign function calls, R code for possible problems

The code: portability, syntax, calls to compiled code, and the static analysis that finds undefined globals and unused variables.

R/

checking Rd files, Rd metadata, Rd line widths, Rd cross-references, for missing documentation entries, for code/documentation mismatches, Rd \usage sections, Rd contents

The documentation: valid Rd, every exported object documented, the usage lines the same as the code, every argument described.

man/, the roxygen comments

checking contents of ‘data’ directory, data for non-ASCII characters, LazyData, data for ASCII and uncompressed saves, R/sysdata.rda

The data files: how they were saved and whether LazyData is consistent.

data/, R/sysdata.rda

vignettes/

@examples, tests/

nothing to fix usually

The same package checked without --as-cran runs a shorter list: the 4.6.1 log of the damaged copy in the next section has no CRAN incoming feasibility, future file timestamps, use of S3 registration, Rd line widths, non-standard things in the check directory or detritus in the temp directory lines, and those six are what --as-cran adds to a package without compiled code. --as-cran also sets defaults for a number of environment variables, which R Internals documents one by one (R Internals: Tools).

The check leaves a directory next to the tarball, shelf.Rcheck, which is worth knowing when a log is not enough. It holds the log 00check.log, the installation log 00install.out, the unpacked source 00_pkg_src, the installed package shelf, the examples as a script (shelf-Ex.R) with their output (shelf-Ex.Rout) and timings, and the test directory with the .Rout files of the tests. The listing is the real one, and shelf inside is the installed package.

ls -1 shelf.Rcheck
ls shelf.Rcheck/shelf
ls shelf.Rcheck/tests

The three lists are, in order, the check directory, the installed package (it is the shelf directory of the check, and its entries are the ones that the binary package listing below explains) and the tests directory with the output of testthat.R. 00check.log is what the console showed, 00install.out is the installation log, shelf-Ex.R is the code of all the examples in one script, 00_pkg_src is the unpacked bundle that was checked, and testthat.Rout is the transcript of the test run.

The incoming checks and the name clash

Without _R_CHECK_CRAN_INCOMING_REMOTE_=false, --as-cran also runs the part of the CRAN incoming checks that needs the network, among them a comparison of the package name with the names of the packages that exist. That is the real result for shelf, and it is an ERROR that no change of code can remove.

R CMD check --as-cran --no-manual shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz
echo "exit status: $?"

Source: Writing R Extensions: Checking packages

* checking CRAN incoming feasibility ... ERROR
Maintainer: ‘Shelf Maintainers <maintainer@example.com>’

New submission

Conflicting package names (submitted: shelf, existing: SHELF [https://CRAN.R-project.org/src/contrib])

Conflicting package names (submitted: shelf, existing: SHELF [CRAN archive])
[...]
Status: 1 ERROR
[...]
exit status: 1

Source: Writing R Extensions: Checking packages

The four lines after the heading say, in order, who the maintainer is, that the package is a new submission (which cran-comments.md mentions when a package is sent), and that a package named SHELF already exists on CRAN, once among the current sources and once in the archive. CRAN compares names without regard to case, so shelf cannot be submitted. The exit status of the command is 1, which the echo line prints; a check that has only warnings or notes exits with 0 (the next section shows one that did), which is why a continuous-integration job needs to read the status line or use the error_on argument that devtools::check() passes on to rcmdcheck. Publishing to CRAN is about what to do with a name that is taken; for the rest of this page _R_CHECK_CRAN_INCOMING_REMOTE_=false is set so that the passing check is the one that is shown.

Options and environment variables

R CMD check --help lists the options that make a check shorter or longer (and says what each does). The ones used on this page are --no-manual, --as-cran, --no-tests, --no-examples and --no-vignettes. The others change what is checked: --run-donttest and --run-dontrun run example code that the author excluded, --run-demo (R 4.5.0) runs the scripts of demo/, --no-codoc skips the comparison of code and documentation, --library and --install-args control the test installation, --timings records how long each example takes, and --use-valgrind and --use-gct are for compiled code.

R Internals documents a long list of environment variables whose names start with _R_CHECK_, each of which switches an individual check on or off. Four matter to a package author. _R_CHECK_FORCE_SUGGESTS_ makes a missing suggested package an error (true by default, false for CRAN submission checks, and set to false by devtools). _R_CHECK_CRAN_INCOMING_ and _R_CHECK_CRAN_INCOMING_REMOTE_ select the incoming checks and the part of them that needs the network, and the second defaults to the value of the first. _R_CHECK_SUGGESTS_ONLY_ and _R_CHECK_DEPENDS_ONLY_ run the examples, tests and vignettes in a library that holds only the declared packages, which is the check that finds a package that was used and not declared. A fifth, NOT_CRAN, is not R’s: testthat’s skip_on_cran() reads it, and the next section shows its effect.

R CMD INSTALL

R CMD INSTALL is the command that every installation goes through: install.packages() for a source package calls it, and so does devtools::install(). It accepts a directory or a tarball, and an option, --library (-l), names the library to install into; without it the first directory of .libPaths() is used. The next commands make a library directory and install the bundle into it, so that nothing else on the machine changes.

mkdir lib
R CMD INSTALL --library=lib shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz

Source: R documentation: INSTALL

* installing *source* package ‘shelf’ ...
** this is package ‘shelf’ version ‘0.1.0’

** R
** data
*** moving datasets to lazyload DB
** inst
** byte-compile and prepare package for lazy loading

*** installing help indices

Source: R Installation and Administration: Installing packages

The lines map onto the work that the install step does, and they are the lines to look for in 00install.out when an installation fails.

Line of the log What it did

** using staged installation

Installs into a temporary directory in the library and moves the package into place when everything worked, so a failed installation does not leave a half-installed package behind (the default since R 3.6.0, --no-staged-install turns it off).

** R

Evaluates the files of R/ once, in a namespace, and saves the result.

** data, *** moving datasets to lazyload DB

Saves each dataset of data/ in a lazy-load database, which is why books costs nothing until it is used.

** inst

Copies inst/ to the top of the installed package, leaving out what .Rinstignore lists.

** byte-compile and prepare package for lazy loading

Byte-compiles the functions (the default since R 3.5.0) and writes R/shelf.rdb and R/shelf.rdx.

** help, *** installing help indices

Converts the Rd files into the help database and the indices.

** building package indices, ** installing vignettes

Writes INDEX and the metadata of Meta/, and installs the built vignettes of inst/doc.

** testing if installed package can be loaded from temporary location, the next line (from final location) and the line about the record of the temporary installation path

Loads the package from the staging directory and from its final place, and checks that nothing in it remembers the temporary path. --no-test-load skips the loading tests.

Source: Writing R Extensions: Package structure

The help text of the command (R CMD INSTALL --help) lists the other switches: --preclean and --clean remove files from earlier or from this installation, --no-docs leaves the help out, --install-tests also installs the tests/ directory (which devtools::install() does by default, as its log showed), --data-compress chooses the compression of the lazy-load database, --byte-compile and --no-byte-compile override the ByteCompile field, --no-test-load skips the loading tests, and --build makes a binary package.

A binary package

--build runs the installation and then packs the installed package into a second tarball in the current directory, a binary package. The name has the operating system and the R series in it, so the real name is shown with its platform part replaced by <platform>. The tarball does not contain R/*.R source; it holds what the installed directory holds.

R CMD INSTALL --library=lib --build shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz
ls *.tar.gz

shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz

The contents of the binary file are the installed package, plus a SHA256 file with the checksums of its files that R 4.6.0 generates by default for --build.

tar tzf shelf_0.1.0_R_<platform>.tar.gz | sed 's#^shelf/##' | sort
