Source: R Installation and Administration: Add-on packages

Reading that list shows what an installed package is made of. DESCRIPTION and NAMESPACE are copied, INDEX and Meta/ are generated, the R code is only in the databases R/shelf.rdb, R/shelf.rdx and the loader R/shelf, the data are in data/Rdata.*, the help pages are in help/shelf.rdb and html/, and the vignette is in doc/. Nothing here can be edited by a reader, which is the point: the installed package is the state in which the code is fixed, and a change to the source needs a new installation.

Using the installed package

The package is now in lib, which is not on R’s library path. R_LIBS is the environment variable whose directories are put at the front of the library path of a new R session, which is the usual way to use a private library from the command line (R_LIBS_USER sets the per-user library, and .libPaths() changes the path inside a running session). The three commands load the package, ask for its version and build a book. The start-up message is printed by library() because .onAttach() ran; since the year is missing, the book is printed with n.d..

R_LIBS=lib Rscript -e 'library(shelf)' -e 'packageVersion("shelf")' -e 'book("Salt and Static", "Mara Quill")'

Source: R documentation: .libPaths, R_LIBS and R_LIBS_USER

shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
[1] ‘0.1.0’
<book> Salt and Static (Mara Quill, n.d.)

Source: R documentation: Rscript

A script that does not want the banner silences it with suppressPackageStartupMessages(), and the option that .onLoad() set is there all the same.

R_LIBS=lib Rscript -e 'suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(shelf))' -e 'getOption("shelf.loan_days")'

Source: R documentation: message, packageStartupMessage and suppressPackageStartupMessages

[1] 21

Source: R documentation: message, packageStartupMessage and suppressPackageStartupMessages

Looking inside an installed package

An installed package can be questioned from R. The script reads the metadata of the installed shelf, lists the names that its namespace exports and the ones that it keeps to itself, and lists what the installed directory, its R/ and its data/ and doc/ subdirectories hold. It runs against the copy of shelf that the earlier R CMD INSTALL put in the scratch library.

# Inspecting an installed package.
packageVersion("shelf")
#> [1] ‘0.1.0’
packageVersion("shelf") >= "0.1.0"
#> [1] TRUE
basename(find.package("shelf"))
#> [1] "shelf"
desc <- packageDescription("shelf")
class(desc)
#> [1] "packageDescription"
desc$Title
#> [1] "Tools for a Small Library Catalogue"
desc$License
#> [1] "MIT + file LICENSE"
desc$Depends
#> [1] "R (>= 4.1.0)"
desc$Maintainer
#> [1] "Shelf Maintainers <maintainer@example.com>"
desc$Author
#> [1] "Shelf Maintainers [aut, cre, cph]"

# DESCRIPTION as installed: the fields the tools added are the last ones.
names(desc)
#>  [1] "Package"                 "Title"
#>  [3] "Version"                 "Authors@R"
#>  [5] "Description"             "License"
#>  [7] "Config/roxygen2/version" "Encoding"
#>  [9] "Roxygen"                 "Suggests"
#> [11] "Config/testthat/edition" "Depends"
#> [13] "VignetteBuilder"         "LazyData"
#> [15] "NeedsCompilation"        "Packaged"
#> [17] "Author"                  "Maintainer"
#> [19] "Built"

# The exports and the internal objects.
sort(getNamespaceExports("shelf"))
#>  [1] "book"            "clean_books"     "clean_loans"     "is_valid_isbn13"
#>  [5] "loan_summary"    "loans_per_month" "new_book"        "normalise_isbn"
#>  [9] "overdue_loans"   "validate_book"
everything <- ls(asNamespace("shelf"), all.names = TRUE)
setdiff(everything, getNamespaceExports("shelf"))
#>  [1] ".__NAMESPACE__."      ".__S3MethodsTable__." ".onAttach"
#>  [4] ".onLoad"              ".packageName"         "format.book"
#>  [7] "isbn_weights"         "print.book"           "print.summary.book"
#> [10] "shelf_today"          "squish"               "summary.book"
shelf:::isbn_weights
#>  [1] 1 3 1 3 1 3 1 3 1 3 1 3 1

# What an installed package directory holds.
sort(list.files(find.package("shelf"), recursive = FALSE))
#>  [1] "CITATION"    "data"        "DESCRIPTION" "doc"         "help"
#>  [6] "html"        "INDEX"       "LICENSE"     "Meta"        "NAMESPACE"
#> [11] "NEWS.md"     "R"
sort(list.files(file.path(find.package("shelf"), "R")))
#> [1] "shelf"       "shelf.rdb"   "shelf.rdx"   "sysdata.rdb" "sysdata.rdx"
sort(list.files(file.path(find.package("shelf"), "data")))
#> [1] "Rdata.rdb" "Rdata.rds" "Rdata.rdx"
sort(list.files(file.path(find.package("shelf"), "doc")))
#> [1] "index.html" "shelf.html" "shelf.R"    "shelf.Rmd"

Source: R documentation: packageDescription and packageVersion

The names of the installed DESCRIPTION show what the tools add to the file that was written: NeedsCompilation, Packaged (who built the bundle and when), Author and Maintainer (derived from Authors@R, as the two lines before the listing show) and Built (the R version, the platform and the date of the installation). The exports are the ten functions of the NAMESPACE. Everything else that the namespace holds is private: the two hooks, the S3 methods (registered in a table and not exported, which is why print.book is in the list and still works for print(b)), shelf_today(), squish(), isbn_weights from R/sysdata.rda, and the three objects that R itself keeps in every namespace (.__NAMESPACE__., .__S3MethodsTable__. and .packageName). The directory listing is the one that the binary package contained: the installed R/ has only databases and a loader, the datasets are in data/Rdata.*, and the built vignette is in doc/.

Running the tests without devtools

The tests of a package are run by R CMD check, as the checking tests line showed, and they can also be run alone against an installed package. tests/testthat.R is an ordinary script: it attaches testthat and the package and calls test_check("shelf"), which finds the testthat/ directory next to it. Running it from the tests directory with the installed package on the library path is what R CMD check does in its own directory. The first run is the one that a check makes: the variable NOT_CRAN is not set, so two tests are skipped: the one in test-loans.R that calls skip_on_cran(), and the snapshot test in test-book.R, because expect_snapshot() is not verified on CRAN. The second sets it, and nothing is skipped.

cd shelf/tests
R_LIBS=../../lib Rscript testthat.R
R_LIBS=../../lib NOT_CRAN=true Rscript testthat.R

Source: testthat package documentation: test_check

shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 2 | PASS 49 ]

══ Skipped tests (2) ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
• On CRAN (2): 'test-book.R:39:1', 'test-loans.R:40:3'

[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 2 | PASS 49 ]
shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 52 ]

Source: testthat package documentation: skip

The summary line of a check with the tests skipped is [ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 2 | PASS 49 ], and the same line is in shelf.Rcheck/tests/testthat.Rout. With nothing skipped it is [ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 52 ], which is what devtools::test() printed in the step before, because devtools::check() sets NOT_CRAN and R CMD check does not.

Reading the output of R CMD check

A passing check is one line, and a failing one is a short list, so the skill to learn is reading the list. Every finding has a level. An ERROR means that a check failed or crashed, and the package is broken in a way that must be fixed. A WARNING is a problem that is very likely to matter, and in principle CRAN admits a package only without warnings (CRAN Repository Policy). A NOTE is something that may be fine and that a submission has to explain in cran-comments.md. The last line of the log, Status:, counts them, and Status: OK means that there is none. The level matters for the exit status of the command, too: in the runs on this page a check with warnings and notes exited with 0, and a check with an ERROR exited with 1.

The real findings below come from deliberately damaged copies of shelf. Each copy was made by copying the finished package, adding the files named in the text, and running the same commands as before. The files that are added are package sources, written to show one mistake each. They sit in a directory of unlinted contrast files, because their purpose is to be wrong: one calls library() inside a function, and one uses a name that is only defined by the package’s data.

A copy with three mistakes in the code

The first copy has three new files in R/ and one stray file at the top level. extra.R exports a function and gives its roxygen block no title, json.R calls jsonlite::toJSON() without declaring jsonlite and attaches stringr with library() inside a function, and titles.R uses the dataset books as if it were a variable.

#' @export
shelf_greeting <- function() {
  "hello from shelf"
}

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: Documenting functions

#' The catalogue as JSON
#'
#' @param x A data frame.
#' @returns A JSON string.
#' @export
to_json <- function(x) {
  jsonlite::toJSON(x)
}

#' Upper-case the titles
#'
#' @param x A character vector.
#' @returns A character vector.
#' @export
shout <- function(x) {
  library(stringr)
  str_to_upper(x)
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Package Dependencies

#' Titles of the catalogue
#'
#' @returns A character vector with the title of every book in [books].
#' @export
catalogue_titles <- function() {
  books$title
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Documenting data sets

The next commands copy the files in, document the package, build it and check it in the default form, without --as-cran. The text of notes.txt, the stray file, is the words "scratch notes". The package is documented first because the new exports must reach NAMESPACE; roxygen2 writes three help pages and none for shelf_greeting(), which has no title.

cp messy/R/*.R shelf/R/
cp messy/notes.txt shelf/
cd shelf && Rscript -e 'devtools::document()'
cd .. && R CMD build shelf
R CMD check --no-manual shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz
echo "exit status: $?"

Source: Writing R Extensions: Checking packages

The check found two warnings and a note. The passing steps are left out of the log, and so is the platform header; the line exit status: 0 at the end is the proof that warnings alone do not change the exit status.

* checking dependencies in R code ... WARNING
'::' or ':::' import not declared from: ‘jsonlite’
'library' or 'require' call not declared from: ‘stringr’
'library' or 'require' call to ‘stringr’ in package code.
  Please use :: or requireNamespace() instead.
  See section 'Suggested packages' in the 'Writing R Extensions' manual.
[...]

[...]

[...]

Source: Writing R Extensions: Package Dependencies

Each finding names its own cause. The first warning has three parts: jsonlite is called with :: and is not declared in DESCRIPTION, stringr is attached with library() and is not declared either, and the library() call itself is not allowed in package code. The note says that two names are used and never defined: books, because the dataset lives in data/ and not in the namespace of the package, and str_to_upper, because the library(stringr) call that would have attached it is hidden from the static analysis. The second warning says that shelf_greeting is an exported object that has no help page. All three are the check doing its job: they are the mistakes that make a package work on the author’s machine and fail on somebody else’s.

Run with --as-cran, the same copy has one more finding, because notes.txt sits at the top level, where R knows no such file.

* checking top-level files ... NOTE
Non-standard file/directory found at top level:
  ‘notes.txt’
[...]
Status: 2 WARNINGs, 2 NOTEs

Source: Writing R Extensions: Checking packages

Fixing them

The fixes are three usethis calls and three small edits. use_package() declares each package in Imports and prints the advice Refer to functions with jsonlite::fun(), use_build_ignore() adds an escaped, anchored pattern to .Rbuildignore, and the three edited files are the fixed versions shown after the output. The calls are a script that was run in the package directory of the copy; its output follows.

# Declare the two packages the code calls with `::`, and keep the scratch
# file out of the tarball. Each call edits one file and says what it did.
usethis::use_package("jsonlite")
#> ✔ Setting active project to
#>   "~/shelf".
#> ✔ Adding jsonlite to 'Imports' field in DESCRIPTION.
#> ☐ Refer to functions with `jsonlite::fun()`.
usethis::use_package("stringr")
#> ✔ Adding stringr to 'Imports' field in DESCRIPTION.
#> ☐ Refer to functions with `stringr::fun()`.
usethis::use_build_ignore("notes.txt")
#> ✔ Adding "^notes\\.txt$" to '.Rbuildignore'.

Source: usethis package documentation: use_package

The edits to the code are small. extra.R gets a title and a @returns line, json.R stops attaching stringr and uses stringr::str_to_upper() with the :: that the new Imports entry now allows, and titles.R writes shelf::books$title, which names the package that the dataset belongs to.

#' A greeting
#'
#' @returns A string.
#' @export
shelf_greeting <- function() {
  "hello from shelf"
}

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: Getting started

#' The catalogue as JSON
#'
#' @param x A data frame.
#' @returns A JSON string.
#' @export
to_json <- function(x) {
  jsonlite::toJSON(x)
}

#' Upper-case the titles
#'
#' @param x A character vector.
#' @returns A character vector.
#' @export
shout <- function(x) {
  stringr::str_to_upper(x)
}

Source: Writing R Extensions: Package Dependencies

#' Titles of the catalogue
#'
#' @returns A character vector with the title of every book in [books].
#' @export
catalogue_titles <- function() {
  shelf::books$title
}

After devtools::document() (which wrote four help pages this time, one more than before), R CMD build and the --as-cran check, the log of the fixed copy ends where a log should: Status: OK. The .Rbuildignore has the fifth line, and Imports lists the two packages.

The note that appears alone: a variable that is not there

The most common single NOTE in a package that has data is the one for a dataset used by its bare name. It is also the one that deserves the most thought, because the static check cannot know that the object exists when the package is attached. The script below puts titles.R of the damaged copy alone into a copy of shelf, documents it and checks it, with the check’s output limited to the summary (quiet = TRUE).

# Run the checks quietly: only the summary is printed at the end.
devtools::document()
#> ℹ Updating shelf documentation
#> ℹ Loading shelf
#> shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
#> Writing 'NAMESPACE'
#> Writing 'catalogue_titles.Rd'
devtools::check(manual = FALSE, quiet = TRUE)
#> ── R CMD check results ──────────────────────────────────────── shelf 0.1.0 ────
#> ❯ checking R code for possible problems ... NOTE
#>   catalogue_titles: no visible binding for global variable ‘books’
#>   Undefined global functions or variables:
#>     books
#> 0 errors ✔ | 0 warnings ✔ | 1 note ✖

Source: devtools package documentation: check

The note names the function and the variable: books is not visible to the package code. It would be found at run time if the package was attached, and not if it was only loaded, so the function would work in the author’s session and fail in a script that called shelf::catalogue_titles() without attaching. The robust form is the one of the fixed copy: name the package, shelf::books, which loads the namespace and reads the lazy-loaded dataset from it. When a name is really a column that a non-standard-evaluation function creates, the other remedy is utils::globalVariables("name"), once, in a file of R/: it tells the check that the name is not an error (R documentation: globalVariables), and it should be reserved for the names that are not objects at all.

Four more mistakes, and the checks that catch them

The second damaged copy shows findings that the first did not. It has a new function, greet(), that is exported with its documentation and whose body calls a helper that was never written; the example in the roxygen block calls it. A second edit then adds an argument to the function and does not run document(), and a third declares stringr in Imports without using it. The string in the function holds a non-ASCII character, written as an escape in the script and saved as UTF-8 in the file. The script is the one that was run in the copy.

# Four ordinary mistakes, made on a copy of the package.
# 1. A new function that calls a helper nobody wrote, with an example.
#    The comments are roxygen2 comments; document() turns them into
#    man/greet.Rd. The string holds a non-ASCII character: it is written
#    here with an escape and saved as UTF-8 bytes (useBytes = TRUE).
writeLines(c(
  "#' Greet a member",
  "#'",
  "#' @param name A member name.",
  "#' @returns A string.",
  "#' @examples",
  "#' greet(\"Ada\")",
  "#' @export",
  "greet <- function(name) {",
  "  paste0(\"Caf\u00e9: \", capitalise(name))",
  "}"
), "R/greet.R", useBytes = TRUE)
roxygen2::roxygenise()
#> ℹ Loading shelf
#> shelf 0.1.0: loan period is 21 days
#> Writing 'NAMESPACE'
#> Writing 'greet.Rd'

# 2. The signature changes, and nobody runs document() again.
code <- readLines("R/greet.R")
old <- "greet <- function(name) {"
code[code == old] <- "greet <- function(name, punct = \"!\") {"
writeLines(code, "R/greet.R")

# 3. A package is declared in Imports and never used.
usethis::use_package("stringr")
#> ✔ Setting active project to
#>   "~/shelf".
#> ✔ Adding stringr to 'Imports' field in DESCRIPTION.
#> ☐ Refer to functions with `stringr::fun()`.

Source: roxygen2 package documentation: Getting started

Source: Writing R Extensions: Checking packages

The messages need little explaining once the files are known. The non-ASCII warning names the file and says what to use instead (\uxxxx escapes), and it names tools::showNonASCIIfile() to find the characters. The note about stringr says that a declared import is never imported from. The note about capitalise is the static analysis seeing a call to a function that does not exist, which is the same message that the damaged json.R produced for str_to_upper. The documentation mismatch shows the code and the documented signature side by side, with the argument that the help page does not know. The example failure is the real error of the example, with the file that holds it: shelf-Ex.R in the check directory. The status line counts the five findings in three levels, and the exit status is 1 because there is an ERROR.

The table collects the messages of this page, each with the text that the tool printed, so that a message found in a log can be looked up here.

A bundle without vignettes

--no-build-vignettes is a time-saver for a quick experiment, and it is a reliable way to meet the two vignette warnings. A copy of the package was built with it and then checked in the default form.

R CMD build --no-build-vignettes shelf
R CMD check --no-manual shelf_0.1.0.tar.gz

Source: R documentation: R CMD build and R CMD check

* checking files in ‘vignettes’ ... WARNING
Files in the 'vignettes' directory but no files in 'inst/doc':
  ‘shelf.Rmd’
[...]

The bundle has vignettes/shelf.Rmd and no inst/doc, so the check warns twice, once for the directory and once for the vignette that has no built output.

package.skeleton(): the older form

Before usethis there was package.skeleton(), a function of the utils package that turns the objects of a workspace into a package directory. The R FAQ dates it to R 1.3.0 and still describes it as the way to set up directories, save data and code and create skeleton help files for a set of functions and datasets. It starts from objects that already exist, which is its good and its bad side: a person who has been working in a session with half a dozen functions gets a package out of them in one call, and a person who starts a package from nothing gets nothing useful from it. The script defines two small functions of the running scenario and makes a package called tinyshelf in the working directory (path = "."), looks at what was created, and removes it.

# package.skeleton() is the older way to start a package: it writes the
# files for objects that already exist in the workspace.
squish <- function(x) gsub(" +", " ", trimws(x))
is_blank <- function(x) is.na(x) | !nzchar(squish(x))

path <- package.skeleton("tinyshelf", list = c("squish", "is_blank"),
                         path = ".")
#> Creating directories ...
#> Creating DESCRIPTION ...
#> Creating NAMESPACE ...
#> Creating Read-and-delete-me ...
#> Saving functions and data ...
#> Making help files ...
#> Done.
#> Further steps are described in './tinyshelf/Read-and-delete-me'.
path
#> [1] "./tinyshelf"

# What it created.
sort(list.files("tinyshelf", recursive = TRUE, all.files = TRUE))
#> [1] "DESCRIPTION"              "man/is_blank.Rd"
#> [3] "man/squish.Rd"            "man/tinyshelf-package.Rd"
#> [5] "NAMESPACE"                "R/is_blank.R"
#> [7] "R/squish.R"               "Read-and-delete-me"

# The generated DESCRIPTION: placeholders to be edited (the Date line is
# today's date and is left out here).
desc <- readLines(file.path("tinyshelf", "DESCRIPTION"))
desc[!startsWith(desc, "Date:")]
#> [1] "Package: tinyshelf"
#> [2] "Type: Package"
#> [3] "Title: What the Package Does (Short Line)"
#> [4] "Version: 1.0"
#> [5] "Authors@R: c(person(\"Givenname\", \"Familyname\", role = c(\"aut\", \"cre\"),"
#> [6] "                    email = \"yourfault@somewhere.net\"),"
#> [7] "             person(\"Anotherone\", \"Ifany\", role = \"ctb\"))"
#> [8] "Description: More about what it does (maybe more than one line)."
#> [9] "License: What license is it under?"

# NAMESPACE lists every export explicitly (since R 4.0.0).
readLines(file.path("tinyshelf", "NAMESPACE"))
#> [1] "export(\"squish\", \"is_blank\")"

# The generated help file for one function is a template full of "~~" notes.
rd <- readLines(file.path("tinyshelf", "man", "squish.Rd"))
rd[1:22]
#>  [1] "\\name{squish}"
#>  [2] "\\alias{squish}"
#>  [3] "%- Also NEED an '\\alias' for EACH other topic documented here."
#>  [4] "\\title{"
#>  [5] "A Capitalized Title (ideally limited to 65 characters)"
#>  [6] "}"
#>  [7] "\\description{"
#>  [8] "%%  ~~ A concise (1-5 lines) description of what the function does. ~~"
#>  [9] "}"
#> [10] "\\usage{"
#> [11] "squish(x)"
#> [12] "}"
#> [13] "%- maybe also 'usage' for other objects documented here."
#> [14] "\\arguments{"
#> [15] "  \\item{x}{"
#> [16] "%%     ~~Describe \\code{x} here~~"
#> [17] "}"
#> [18] "}"
#> [19] "\\details{"
#> [20] "%%  ~~ If necessary, more details than the description above ~~"
#> [21] "}"
#> [22] "\\value{"
length(rd)
#> [1] 61

# Some of the lines of the instructions file it leaves behind.
readLines(file.path("tinyshelf", "Read-and-delete-me"))[c(1, 3, 4, 8, 9)]
#> [1] "* Edit the help file skeletons in 'man', possibly combining help files"
#> [2] "* Edit the package 'DESCRIPTION'."
#> [3] "* Edit the exports in 'NAMESPACE', and add necessary imports."
#> [4] "* Run R CMD build to build the package tarball."
#> [5] "* Run R CMD check to check the package tarball."

# Clean up.
unlink("tinyshelf", recursive = TRUE)
dir.exists("tinyshelf")
#> [1] FALSE

Source: R documentation: package.skeleton

Reading the output is a short course in what a source package contains. The directory has a DESCRIPTION, a NAMESPACE, one R file for each function (R/squish.R, R/is_blank.R), one Rd file for each function and one more for the package (man/tinyshelf-package.Rd), and a file called Read-and-delete-me that lists the next steps. The DESCRIPTION is a set of placeholders that have to be edited (a title, a version of 1.0, two made-up authors and a licence field that asks "What license is it under?"). The NAMESPACE lists every function in one export() line, since R 4.0.0 (R NEWS: Changes in R 4.0.0: package.skeleton() now explicitly lists all exports in the NAMESPACE file), and the instruction file that the function leaves behind says to edit the exports and to add the necessary imports. The Rd files are templates full of ~~ notes that tell the author what to write. The function returns the path of the new directory invisibly since R 4.6.0 (R NEWS: Changes in R 4.6.0), which is why the script prints path explicitly, and the same release lets it create a blank skeleton without any objects.

The skeleton is not a package that passes a check, and the real log shows how far it is from one. The commands below build it and check it without any edit.

Rscript -e 'squish <- function(x) gsub(" +", " ", trimws(x))' -e 'package.skeleton("tinyshelf", list = "squish")'
R CMD build tinyshelf
R CMD check --no-manual tinyshelf_1.0.tar.gz

Source: Writing R Extensions: Checking packages

* checking DESCRIPTION meta-information ... WARNING
Non-standard license specification:
  What license is it under?
Standardizable: FALSE
[...]
* checking Rd files ... NOTE
prepare_Rd: squish.Rd:7-9: Dropping empty section \description
[...]
prepare_Rd: tinyshelf-package.Rd:33-35: Dropping empty section \examples
[...]
* checking Rd contents ... NOTE
Rd files without \description:
  ‘squish.Rd’
Argument items with no description in Rd file 'squish.Rd':
  ‘x’
Auto-generated content requiring editing in Rd file 'squish.Rd':
  \title: ‘A Capitalized Title (ideally limited to 65 characters)’
[...]
Status: 1 WARNING, 2 NOTEs

Source: Writing R Extensions: Checking packages

Three things stand out. The licence field is not a standard specification, and that is a WARNING. The Rd files have empty sections that the check drops (the prepare_Rd lines name each of them, and only the first and the last are shown), and the Rd contents check recognises the template: an argument item with no description, and an auto-generated title that still says "A Capitalized Title". NOTEs and WARNINGs are what a person has to remove before the package is real, and the 1.0 version, the made-up authors and the missing tests are what the check does not know about. The longer way round with usethis and roxygen2 gets the same files with less to delete, which is why it replaced the skeleton, and the table of the workflow section shows the one-to-one mapping.

The functions that package.skeleton() calls are available separately for a single object: prompt() writes a skeleton Rd file for a function, promptData() for a data frame and promptPackage() for the package overview. The Rd files that they write are the ones that roxygen2 now generates from comments (R documentation: prompt, promptData, promptPackage), and a package that is maintained with roxygen2 should not also keep hand-edited copies: the generated file starts with a line that says not to edit it by hand, and devtools::document() rewrites it.

Pitfalls

  • Editing a generated file. NAMESPACE and every file of man/ start with "Generated by roxygen2: do not edit by hand", and the next devtools::document() overwrites them (or, for a NAMESPACE without that line, refuses to touch it and leaves a hand-written file that then disagrees with the code). Change the comment in R/ instead, and commit the generated files, because CRAN needs them in the bundle.

  • Top-level code that runs once. The files of R/ are evaluated when the package is installed, so a value computed at the top level of a file, such as today’s date, is the value of the day of the installation. Wrap such a value in a function (shelf_today() does), or compute it in .onLoad(), which runs at every load.

  • library() or require() inside package code. Both attach a package as a side effect of calling your function. Declare the package in Imports and call it with ::, or test for a suggested package with requireNamespace("pkg", quietly = TRUE). The check reports the call.

  • Using Depends for convenience. A package in Depends is attached for every user, so the user’s search path changes and masking follows (see Packages, Libraries and Namespaces). The one entry that belongs there for most packages is R (>= x.y.z).

  • Changing a signature and not running document(). The usage line of the Rd file no longer matches the function, and the check warns about the mismatch (the real message is in the table of the check section).

  • Reading files by a path relative to the source tree. file.path("inst", "extdata", "books.csv") works under load_all() and fails when the package is installed. Use system.file("extdata", "books.csv", package = "shelf") and test the result with nzchar(), because it returns "" for a file that is not there.

  • Checking the directory and not the bundle. R CMD check shelf works on the directory and does not run every check: the checks of the package subdirectories, for example, are on by default only for a tarball (R CMD check --help). The tarball is what CRAN and the users receive, so build first (R CMD build, or devtools::check(), which builds first).

  • Forgetting that tests are skipped on CRAN. R CMD check leaves NOT_CRAN unset, so tests that call skip_on_cran() do not run and snapshot tests are not verified, and the summary line says SKIP 2; devtools::check() sets NOT_CRAN=true, so they do run. A test that passes under one and fails under the other is a real finding, not a flake.

  • Unanchored .Rbuildignore patterns. The lines are regular expressions matched anywhere in the path: data-raw also removes R/data-raw-helpers.R. Anchor with ^ and $ and escape the dots, or let usethis::use_build_ignore() write the line.

  • Output at load time. A package that prints with cat() or print() when it is loaded cannot be silenced. Use packageStartupMessage() in .onAttach(), and print nothing in .onLoad().

  • A dataset that is not documented. Every dataset of data/ needs a help page (the roxygen block above a string with the name of the dataset), and the check reports the object that has none.

  • Choosing a name last. A package name that exists on CRAN in any capitalisation cannot be submitted, as the real check of shelf showed. Look the name up before the package has a hundred commits (Publishing to CRAN shows how).

  • Installing into the system library. An installation by an administrator changes the packages of every user, and a later update of R can orphan them. Use a per-user or per-project library (R_LIBS_USER, --library, renv), which Reproducible Environments with renv covers.

  • Installing a package and not finding it. A package installed into a library that the session does not search is not found by library(). Check .libPaths() and the --library or lib argument that was used; R FAQ 7.30, "I installed a package but the functions are not there", is the entry for this case.

Version notes

The entries come from the NEWS files of R (R NEWS; the entries before R 3.6.1 are in R NEWS: Changes in R 3.x), from the R FAQ and from the NEWS of the add-on packages, which are named in the first column when they apply. The searches covered the NEWS of R 3.5.0 to 4.6.1 for package.skeleton, R CMD build, R CMD INSTALL, R CMD check, NAMESPACE, DESCRIPTION and the serialization format.

Version Change

R 1.3.0

package.skeleton() is added (R FAQ 5.5).

R 2.14.0 (October 2011)

Every package has a namespace; the LazyLoad field of DESCRIPTION is ignored from here on (Writing R Extensions).

R 3.0.0

The transitional support for installing packages without a namespace is removed: R CMD build still adds one, and a .First.lib() function is ignored.

R 3.5.0

All packages are byte-compiled on installation by default. Serialization format version 3 appears, which R versions before 3.5.0 cannot read, and it is why usethis::use_data() files make R CMD build add R (>= 3.5.0) to a package that does not state its R requirement. package.skeleton() gets an encoding argument.

R 3.6.0

Source packages are installed with the staged installation by default (--no-staged-install turns it off). Serialization format 3 becomes the default of save(). A NAMESPACE can register S3 methods for a generic of another package with S3method(pkg::gen, cls), which delays the registration until that package is loaded.

R 4.0.0

package.skeleton() lists all exports explicitly in the NAMESPACE it writes.

R 4.1.0

The native pipe and the function shorthand \(x) arrive; R CMD build adds Depends: R (>= 4.1.0) when the code uses either and the field is missing, and says so. R CMD build omits tarballs and binaries of earlier builds of the same package from the new one. R CMD check gains sanity checks of LazyData.

R 4.2.0

R CMD build skips the temporary installation for a package whose only dynamic Rd content is the \doi macro, and gives a smaller tarball. R CMD check --as-cran validates the HTML made from the Rd files.

R 4.3.0

Installing a package parses every R/*.R file separately, so a syntax error names the file and the line. R CMD check reports problems when reading NEWS.md.

R 4.4.0

R CMD build of a package with no NAMESPACE creates one with the recommended exportPattern("^[^.]") instead of exporting everything. tools::checkRd() reports a title that ends with a period (ignored by R CMD check unless a minimum level is asked for), and R CMD check warns about non-ASCII characters in NAMESPACE and notes Rd files without an alias. R CMD build --user= overrides the user name recorded in Packaged.

R 4.5.0

R CMD check --run-demo checks the scripts of demo/, and R CMD check --as-cran notes bad parts of the URL fields of DESCRIPTION. R CMD build --compression=zstd is available where zstd is supported.

R 4.6.0

Package README.md files are installed and shown in the HTML help. package.skeleton() returns the path invisibly and can make a blank skeleton. R CMD INSTALL --build writes a SHA256 file by default, and R CMD build --sha256 can add one to a tarball. R CMD check on a tarball no longer takes the package name from the file name.

roxygen2 8.0.0 (2026-05-01)

Options can be set in Config/roxygen2/ fields (Config/roxygen2/markdown: TRUE), the old Roxygen: field is still supported, and the version is stored in Config/roxygen2/version instead of RoxygenNote; roxygen2 migrates the field on the next document(). Documenting a value such as x <- 1:10 no longer adds data-set markup: a dataset is documented by a block above a string with its name. The page was checked against roxygen2 8.1.1.

usethis 3.2.2

Still writes Roxygen: list(markdown = TRUE) for a new package, next to the new version field.

devtools 2.5.0

create() is deprecated in favour of usethis::create_package(), as the body of the function shows (lifecycle::deprecate_warn("2.5.0", ...)). devtools 2.5.2 no longer exports the use_*() functions: they are usethis’s.

Source: R NEWS: Changes in R 3.5.0 to 4.6.1

The R 4.6.2 entries that exist in the R-devel NEWS are bug fixes only and none concerns the package tools on this page. R-devel (the upcoming 4.7.0) was not run here.
